catalogTitle: עליית שלש קליפות הטמאות - ע"י ביטול בששים' או תשובה מאהבה - זהו ניצוץ מימות המשיח. אין מציאות כתקלה עולמית.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that teshuvah out of love draws a flash of the days of Moshiach into a person's own world, which is why it can repair even what the Tanya calls beyond repair, and shows that Hashem never lets a sin become a mishap for the whole world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews Tanya chapter 7: forbidden relations create a body and cannot be repaired except in the future or by great teshuvah out of love, which brings a flash of the days of Moshiach. He compares it to a lightning flash in the night and to Chanukah, when the light of Moshiach is revealed at the lighting. Hashem's domain is reshus hayachid and the klipah's is reshus harabim; Shabbos centers on hotza'ah, and Chanukah lights a candle in reshus harabim. Chanukah comes from Binah, the root of teshuvah out of love. He then explains why even such teshuvah cannot instantly repair a mamzer, and why a mamzer still dies through sustained teshuvah. Turning to Tanya chapter 8, he discusses forbidden food eaten unknowingly, the Tzemach Tzedek's link to the Rambam and the Mechaber, and why the Mishnah Berurah ruled like the Ra'avad: so that the cantonist children could still do teshuvah.

en: Following Tanya chapter 7, the Mashgiach explains that forbidden relations cannot be repaired except in the future or by great teshuvah out of love, which already now draws a taste of the days of Moshiach.
Hashem's domain is reshus hayachid and the domain of the sitra achra is reshus harabim, which is why carrying out (hotza'ah) is the core of Shabbos.
Chanukah is a flash of the days of Moshiach in the darkness of exile, lighting a light in reshus harabim and turning Har Eisav into Har Tziyon.
Teshuvah out of love is Binah, the source of Chanukah, and one who does it lives the days of Moshiach in his own small world.
A mamzer cannot be repaired by a moment of teshuvah, but sustained teshuvah out of love can repair it, and then the mamzerim die; there is no situation in which a Jew's path to repair is closed.
The Mashgiach explains that the Mishnah Berurah's ruling, that forbidden food eaten unknowingly can be elevated, was guided by Heaven so that the cantonist children could later do teshuvah.

title.en: Teshuvah out of love as a flash of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews Tanya chapter 7: forbidden relations create a body and have no repair except in the future or by great teshuvah out of love, which brings a taste of the days of Moshiach. He compares this to a lightning flash in the night and to Chanukah, when, as the Bnei Yissaschar brings, the light of Moshiach is revealed at the lighting.

title.en: Reshus hayachid and reshus harabim

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what Chanukah and the days of Moshiach are, bringing the haftarah's verse that saviors will judge Har Eisav from Har Tziyon. He explains that Hashem's domain is reshus hayachid and the klipah's is reshus harabim, and shows from Maseches Shabbos and the verse 'let no man leave his place' that hotza'ah is the heart of Shabbos.

title.en: Kislev: lighting a candle in reshus harabim

summary.en: Kislev opens with Yaakov leaving the reshus hayachid of Eretz Yisrael for reshus harabim, and its avodah is to light a candle there, the light of Moshiach, until all becomes reshus hayachid in the day that is wholly Shabbos. He adds that the twenty-four days before Chanukah lead into it, as the sefarim count them against the letters of Baruch Shem and Shema Yisrael.

title.en: Binah, Chanukah and teshuvah out of love

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah comes from Binah, eight levels above Malchus, and that teshuvah out of love is Binah while teshuvah out of fear is Malchus. One who does teshuvah out of love brings the days of Moshiach into his own small world, and can therefore repair even forbidden relations and forbidden foods.

title.en: Why a mamzer needs sustained teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why even teshuvah out of love cannot instantly repair a mamzer: the sin lives on in another body, a process the klipah dug into time. He brings the tradition that through great sustained teshuvah the mamzerim die, stresses that no Jew's path to repair is ever closed, and adds that Hashem also does not reveal families whose taint was forgotten.

title.en: Hashem's world cannot be ruined

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the nations' worry about pollution of air, water and the earth with the Jew's belief that Hashem created and runs the world and it cannot be ruined. A Jew's worry is to learn, daven, give tzedakah and have good middos; he brings the generation of the Tower, who worried about the heavens, against Avraham Avinu.

title.en: Forbidden foods and aveirah lishmah

summary.en: Returning to Tanya chapter 8, the Mashgiach explains that forbidden foods are bound in the klipah, so even eaten unknowingly for the sake of Heaven they do not rise, and a true issur will be removed only in the days of Moshiach. He explains what an aveirah lishmah is, when it was permitted, and why eating forbidden food unknowingly is not one.

title.en: The Tzemach Tzedek, the Rambam and the Ra'avad

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Tzemach Tzedek in Derech Mitzvosecha, who ties the Tanya's statement to the Rambam and the Mechaber, who rule that one who ate forbidden food unknowingly does not make a bracha acharonah, against the Ra'avad. Since a bracha elevates the food, no bracha means no elevation, while the Mishnah Berurah rules like the Ra'avad.

title.en: Why the Mishnah Berurah ruled otherwise

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Mishnah Berurah ruled differently and answers that nothing happens by chance: halachos follow each generation's sages, as with Rabbi Eliezer's view on preparations for milah and Beis Shammai's rulings in the days of Moshiach. In the Mishnah Berurah's time the Russian government forced thousands of cantonist children to eat forbidden food, and Heaven guided his ruling so that they could still do teshuvah.

catalogTitle: Rectifying the Months of תמוז and אב (connection to פרשת שלח)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tamuz and Av, the months of the meraglim and of strict judgment, are meant to be transformed, through guarding the eyes and remembering that each person is Hashem's shaliach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the letter combination of Tamuz, drawn from Haman's words 'v'chol zeh einenu shoveh li': fully reversed and from the final letters, it marks Tamuz as the hardest month, a month of strict judgment. Because it comes from the Megillah of 'v'nahapoch hu', the task is to transform it, and Chof-Gimmel Sivan, the day of the good news in the Megillah, falls this year on the Shabbos of blessing Tamuz. He touches on Parshas Shelach's challah and nesachim as the return of the kallah, then explains the meraglim: they went in days of judgment, and their delay for Miriam brought them back on Tisha B'Av, which holds the birth of Moshiach. Tamuz and Av are the two eyes; the meraglim blemished seeing, so these months bring trials of the eyes. Finally, everyone is Hashem's shaliach, and a person's name is his shlichus; summer vacation should be used to see Hashem in nature.

en: The letter combination of Tamuz comes from Haman's words in the Megillah, fully reversed and from the final letters, marking it as the hardest month of strict judgment, which must be transformed as in 'v'nahapoch hu'.
Chof-Gimmel Sivan, the day the good news of 'v'nahapoch hu' went out, falls on the Shabbos when Tamuz is blessed, a sign to use it to transform the month.
The meraglim went in days of strict judgment; waiting for Miriam brought their return to Tisha B'Av, which the Mashgiach calls a day with a good inner side, the birth of Moshiach.
Tamuz and Av are the two eyes; the meraglim blemished seeing, so these months carry the greatest trials of the eyes, and one who wants to stay bound to Hashem must guard his eyes in them.
Every person is a shaliach sent down by Hashem to bring up Torah and mitzvos, and his name carries his shlichus; the yetzer hara works to make him forget it.
The summer vacation should be used as Hashem wants, including seeing His creation in nature and coming through it to love and awe of Him, as the Rambam describes.

title.en: Tamuz, the hardest month

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the letter combination of Tamuz, from Haman's 'v'chol zeh einenu shoveh li', is fully reversed and from final letters, worse than Av's, so the whole month is judgment. He says the answer is not to sulk but to transform it, which is why its combination comes from the Megillah of 'v'nahapoch hu'.

title.en: Chof-Gimmel Sivan, a day of transformation

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions the custom not to make weddings after the twenty-second of the month, and that the Chiddushei HaRim and the Divrei Chaim made weddings on Chof-Gimmel Sivan because of its standing. It is the day the good news of 'v'nahapoch hu' went out, and this year it is the Shabbos of blessing Tamuz, a sign to use it to transform the month.

title.en: Challah and nesachim: the kallah returns

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Shelach a hard sedra of the meraglim but also a good one, with challah and nesachim. He brings the Zohar's parable of a king who sent his kallah away three times, the last time to a foul place, where he himself comes to bring her back, and connects nesachim and challah to the place of the Beis HaMikdash from which Adam and Chava were taken.

title.en: The meraglim in days of judgment

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the meraglim went in Tamuz and Av, days of judgment, bringing the Rema MiPano's reading of 'bikurei anavim' as hinting to the Satan, and adds that the Tamuz combination equals 'yemei bikurei anavim' in gematria. He brings the Satmar Rav that waiting for Miriam brought the return on Tisha B'Av, which turns out to be good, since it is the day of Moshiach's birth.

title.en: Mechiyas Amalek before every Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that wiping out Amalek precedes every building of the Mikdash: Amalek before the Mishkan, Shaul's war on Erev Pesach, Mordechai before the second Beis HaMikdash, and again before Moshiach. He then asks how Shaul could say 'hakimosi es dvar Hashem', and explains that by leaving Agag alive Haman came into the world, leading to Purim and 'kiymu v'kiblu'.

title.en: Why waiting for Miriam was a blessing

summary.en: In the same way, the Mashgiach asks what would have happened had they not waited for Miriam: the meraglim, sent on the twenty-ninth of Sivan, would have left on Chof-Gimmel Sivan and blemished that day forever. So the delay was a blessing, and Tamuz, rooted in lashon hara, must be transformed like Purim.

title.en: Tamuz and Av, the two eyes

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings, he thinks from the Bnei Yissaschar, that Tamuz and Av are the two eyes of the year, hinted in 'eini eini yordah mayim'. The meraglim blemished seeing, so these months bring the greatest trials of the eyes; he brings the Gemara in Bava Basra on one who shuts his eyes from evil and the Midrash on 'am naval', applying them to the streets today.

title.en: The two nesi'im of Tamuz and Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach matches the twelve nesi'im to the months: the two who sinned, Elitzur ben Shdeiur of Reuven in Korach's dispute and Shlumiel ben Tzurishaddai of Shimon, who was Zimri, belong to Tamuz and Av. 'Otzem einav me're'os bera' equals their names in gematria, and the eyes must be rectified until 'ayin b'ayin yiru'. He adds a story of tears on Tisha B'Av and a word on holding the Kiddush cup like a rose.

title.en: Summer travel and our shlichus

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that everyone travels in Tamuz and Av, a season of sending, and brings the Chasam Sofer that both Hashem and the people sent the meraglim. Every person is a shaliach: the neshamos sang above until Hashem sent them down to bring up the gems of Torah and mitzvos, yet people rushing in the street forget who sent them.

title.en: A person's name is his shlichus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the angel of Esav would not tell Yaakov his name: a person's name is his shlichus, which is why one says a passuk of his name after Shemoneh Esrei. The yetzer hara wants people to forget their name and their mission, so he urges a cheshbon hanefesh this Shabbos and to say one is the shaliach of Hashem alone.

title.en: Using the vacation to see Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach takes leave until after the summer and tells the bochurim to use the vacation as Hashem wants: exercise and swimming are fine, but it is no time to throw off the yoke. In the city tall buildings block the sky, while in the country one should look at trees, streams and butterflies and come, as the Rambam writes, to love of Hashem.

title.en: A tzaddik's last look at creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a great tzaddik who, in his last days in a Tel Aviv hospital, asked to be carried to the garden to see Hashem's creation once more, and of another who davened looking out at the fields. He closes with 'se'u marom eineichem', the Rambam on awe through creation, and blessings for a healthy summer and the great 'v'nahapoch hu'.

catalogTitle: עונשים -על הנאה גשמיות' לעם הארץ שמבטל תורה' לתלמיד חכם המבטל תורה; לימוד חכמת חיצוניות יותר חמור מדברים בטלים.

oneLiner.en: Continuing Tanya chapter 8, the Mashgiach explains the lasting imprint of physical pleasure and idle talk, the special severity of bitul Torah for one who can learn, and why secular wisdom studied for its own sake is worse than idle talk, permitted only as a means for the sake of Heaven.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues Tanya chapter 8. Forbidden food comes from the three impure kelipos, and even a rabbinic prohibition rests on the food itself. Kosher food eaten for pleasure falls temporarily into kelipas noga; even if later elevated, an imprint remains in the body, like a stain that survives washing, and only chibut hakever removes it, unless one, like Rebbi, never enjoyed this world. Idle talk of an am ha'aretz is kelipas noga, cleansed by kaf hakela; a talmid chacham who could learn commits bitul Torah, with its own severe punishment, beyond the cold Gehinom for neglected positive mitzvos. Secular wisdom is worse than idle talk: idle talk comes from the middos, as animals chatter, while wisdom comes from chabad that fell into kelipah at the breaking of the vessels. It is allowed only as a means, for parnassah or serving Hashem, with honest calculations and never through studies bound up with heresy and sin.

en: Kosher food eaten for pleasure falls into kelipas noga, and even after it is elevated an imprint remains in the body that only chibut hakever removes.
Idle talk of one who cannot learn is kelipas noga, while for a talmid chacham who could learn it is the sin of bitul Torah, with its own severe punishment.
Studying secular wisdom when one could learn Torah is worse than idle talk, because it clothes the soul's chabad in kelipah.
Secular wisdom reached the nations through the breaking of the vessels, when chochmah fell into the kelipos.
Torah must be learned for its own sake, while secular wisdom may be learned only as a means, for parnassah or to serve Hashem.
The permission has two conditions: the intent must be for the sake of Heaven, and the studies may not be bound up with prohibitions such as heresy.

title.en: Forbidden food and the impure kelipos

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya on forbidden food, which cannot be elevated, and mentions the Tzemach Tzedek's notes on rabbinic prohibitions, explaining that even a rabbinic prohibition rests on the food itself. He contrasts the desire for forbidden things, from the gentile 'demons' of the impure kelipos, with the desire for kosher things, which can be elevated.

title.en: The imprint of permitted pleasure

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that kosher food eaten for pleasure enters kelipas noga and leaves an imprint in the body even after teshuvah, like a stain that survives washing, removed only by chibut hakever. He brings Rebbi, who raised his ten fingers and said he had not enjoyed this world, though he was very wealthy, as Rashi in Toldos shows.

title.en: Idle talk: the am ha'aretz and the talmid chacham

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the idle talk of an am ha'aretz who cannot learn is not itself a sin, but is kelipas noga and needs cleansing by kaf hakela. A talmid chacham who could learn commits bitul Torah, and the Mashgiach explains the fire Gehinom for active sins, the snow Gehinom for neglected positive mitzvos, and a special punishment for bitul Torah.

title.en: Secular wisdom counts as idle talk

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya that the wisdom of the nations is included in idle talk regarding bitul Torah, and is worse. Mathematics or physics studied when one could learn is idle talk compared to Torah. He brings Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya to show that the wisdom of the nations rises and falls opposite the sages of Torah.

title.en: Earlier generations' depth, today's details

summary.en: In a digression the Mashgiach observes that recent generations developed pilpul and new chiddushim, while the earlier Rishonim had deeper knowledge; likewise the nations' earlier wise men pursued wisdom for its own sake, while today's science is details and machinery. A doctor once knew a patient's state from his face and pulse; today it is tests and electronics.

title.en: Idle talk from the middos, wisdom from chabad

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that empty chatter comes from the middos, as animals bark and sing, while wisdom comes from chabad, and kelipah too has chabad. So one who studies secular wisdom to be a scientist when he could learn does greater damage than one who tells jokes, since the impurity reaches the soul's chabad. He then rereads the Tanya's words on this.

title.en: The breaking of the vessels

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the beginning of Tanya chapter 3: the seven middos have good and evil, while chabad is only good. He explains, calling it an awesome matter, that at the breaking of the vessels chochmah fell into the kelipos, which is why the nations have wisdom, and why engaging in it gives the kelipah a hold on something from a very high place.

title.en: Torah lishmah, secular wisdom only as a means

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the exception: one who studies secular wisdom for parnassah, to support his family in Torah and to learn, elevates it like eating for the sake of Heaven. Torah must be learned lishmah and never as a spade, as the Mishnah says, while secular wisdom must be learned as a spade, not for its own sake; a better-paying profession can leave more time to learn.

title.en: All wisdom is found in the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the reason of the Rambam and Ramban for studying these wisdoms: to serve Hashem, such as drawing people closer to Torah. He adds that they knew the wisdoms from the Torah itself, citing the Ramban's introduction to Chumash, and points to tzaddikim whom doctors consulted and Rebbes who wrote prescriptions without schooling, since one who learns lishmah knows everything.

title.en: Honest calculations and the two conditions

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns that the intent must be honest: few who study medicine do so for chessed, and many calculations about parnassah are false. An aveirah cannot be done lishmah, so college, where one must study heresy and faces tests of immorality, has no heter even for parnassah. He concludes with two conditions: intent for the sake of Heaven and studies free of prohibitions.

catalogTitle: התחלת התשובה' על דרך עבודה' לתרץ הקושיות שבראש הספר. רשע ורע לו צדיק ורע לו (הרע כפוף בו) צדיק וטוב לו מהותם.

oneLiner.en: Opening Tanya chapter 10, the Mashgiach explains the tzaddik gamur, who has turned his evil into good and hates this world's pleasures out of love of Hashem, the tzaddik she'eino gamur, whose evil is only subdued, and the bnei aliyah who raise the evil up and serve Hashem for the sake of the Shechinah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach explains that until chapter 10 the Tanya laid down foundations; now the path of avodah begins, and the questions of chapter one on tzaddik v'tov lo and tzaddik v'ra lo will be answered. The tzaddik gamur and the rasha gamur are two extremes that have lost their bechirah: one has turned his evil into good, the other, like Pharaoh, his good into evil. He tells of tzaddikim who remembered earlier gilgulim. The tzaddik gamur hates this world's pleasures because they come from the sitra achra and are the opposite of his love of Hashem with delight, illustrated by stories of the Beis Aharon and the Berditchever. The tzaddik she'eino gamur hates evil only according to his level; his evil is subdued and nullified, not transformed. Finally he explains the bnei aliyah, who raise the evil up to holiness and serve Hashem for a need on High, to do kindness with the Shechinah in exile.

en: From chapter 10 the Tanya moves from foundations to the path of avodah and begins answering the questions of chapter one.
The tzaddik gamur has transformed his evil into good, while the rasha gamur has transformed his good into evil; both extremes no longer have real bechirah.
The tzaddik gamur hates the pleasures of this world because they come from the kelipah, the opposite of his love of Hashem with delight.
In the tzaddik she'eino gamur the evil is subdued and nullified by the good, but it remains evil, so he is called tzaddik v'ra lo.
Hatred of evil and love of Hashem go together: only one who hates evil completely can love Hashem completely.
The bnei aliyah raise the evil up to holiness, and they serve Hashem not to quench their own thirst for Him but to do kindness with the Shechinah in exile.

title.en: From foundations to the path of avodah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that until chapter 10 the Tanya laid down foundations, and from here the path of avodah begins and the questions of chapter one are answered. He reads the opening of the chapter and sets out the two extremes: the tzaddik gamur who has turned his yetzer hara into good, and the rasha who has turned his good into evil.

title.en: Pharaoh, and tzaddikim without bechirah

summary.en: Using Pharaoh, whose heart was turned to evil, the Mashgiach shows that the two extremes have lost their bechirah. He tells of tzaddikim such as the Yismach Moshe and the Apter Rav who remembered their earlier gilgulim, and explains that Pharaoh let the Jews go not by free choice; until Matan Torah, he adds, non-Jews could still reach a high level, as the Ramchal discusses.

title.en: Tzaddik v'ra lo and tzaddik v'tov lo

summary.en: After placing the beinoni between the extremes, the Mashgiach reads the Tanya: one who drives out evil but has not transformed it is a tzaddik she'eino gamur, tzaddik v'ra lo, whose evil is only bent and suppressed. The tzaddik gamur has turned it fully to good, has removed the soiled garments, and despises the pleasures of this world.

title.en: Love of Hashem with delight

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the tzaddik gamur hates this world's pleasures: they come from the kelipah, while he serves Hashem with a love full of delight. He brings the Beis Aharon on the word 'kamah', his reply about a nobleman who went sledding on sugar in summer, a tzaddik who could not tear himself away from Shemoneh Esrei, and the Berditchever who rushed to learn Gemara Sukkah after Yom Kippur; the measure of the love is the measure of the hatred of the sitra achra.

title.en: Why we must know what a tzaddik is

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why people who are not tzaddikim need to know this, and answers that one must love tzaddikim and know whose Torah one learns. The tzaddik she'eino gamur hates this world only according to his level, which he illustrates with the countless levels among people; one should not be shaken by still feeling an attraction to this world, since fighting it is our avodah. He returns to the tzaddikim who remembered earlier gilgulim and explains why others are not given that memory.

title.en: Evil nullified, and the levels of tzaddikim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the tzaddik she'eino gamur the evil is nullified by the strength of the good so that he never sins, yet it remains evil, and so he is tzaddik v'ra lo; one who does not hate evil completely does not love Hashem completely, except at high moments. This level divides into countless levels, from those whose evil is batel b'shishim, which he connects with the Gemara's numbers of 18,000, 36 and one tzaddik.

title.en: The bnei aliyah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the true tzaddikim gemurim are called bnei aliyah: they raise the evil up to holiness, as in the Zohar's story of R' Chiya at the heichal of R' Shimon bar Yochai, where darkness is turned to light. A second reason is that they serve Hashem for a need on High, not even to quench their own thirst for Him, but to do kindness with the Shechinah in exile, as the Tikkunim and the Ra'aya Mehemna describe.

catalogTitle: מלחמת יצה"ר ויצה"ט על העיר הקטנה. שניהם רוצים שהשני יהיה בטל אצלו.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains how the Godly soul and the animal soul fight like two kings over the 'small city' of the body, each wanting the other to be subdued to it, and what this war asks of an ordinary person.

abstract.en: Learning Tanya chapter 9, the Mashgiach explains that the animal soul of a Jew, from kelipas nogah, dwells in the blood-filled left chamber of the heart, while the Godly soul dwells in the brain and the right chamber. The heart's blood even drives the brain to scheme for the heart's desires; the liver, all blood, is lower still, and a Midrash reads Pharaoh's 'heavy heart' as a heart that was really a liver. Contemplation of Hashem's greatness gives birth to love, as Birchas Yotzer leads to Ahavah Rabbah. The body is a small city over which the yetzer tov and the yetzer hara wage constant war, each wanting the other subdued. The yetzer tov wants its love to overflow into the left chamber until even appetite serves Hashem, as with matzah eaten with appetite. Only a tzaddik gamur transforms his evil; for most people the avodah is to subdue it, and the Zohar's parable shows the yetzer hara itself serves the King.

en: The animal soul dwells in the blood-filled left chamber of the heart, and the Godly soul dwells in the brain and spreads to the right chamber, where there is hardly any blood.
The desires of the heart rise to the brain and drive it to scheme how to fulfil them, because the heart sends its blood to the brain.
The body is a small city over which the Godly soul and the animal soul wage a lifelong war, each wanting the whole body subjugated to it alone.
The yetzer tov wants the love born of contemplation to fill the right chamber and overflow into the left, so that even the bad inclinations are subdued and used for good.
Only a tzaddik gamur transforms his yetzer hara into good; for the vast majority of people the avodah is to subdue it, like a king who imprisons the enemy king.
The yetzer hara itself is there for a person's good: like the harlot in the Zohar's parable, its true wish is that the person withstand it.

title.en: The animal soul in the left chamber of the heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's words that the animal soul of a Jew, from kelipas nogah, dwells in the blood-filled left chamber of the heart. He explains the two chambers, the blood as the vehicle of the vital soul, and why a Jew's animal soul can be transformed to good.

title.en: Desires rise to the brain; the Godly soul's seat

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains how the desires of the heart spread through the body and rise to the brain, which plans how to fulfil them because the heart's blood drives it. He then reads that the Godly soul dwells in the brain and in the right chamber, 'the heart of the wise is on his right'.

title.en: The liver, and Pharaoh's heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the liver, lower than heart and brain, is full of blood, which is why the poskim say it cannot be salted but must be roasted. He tells the Midrash of the lion, the donkey that had 'no heart' and the fox, and the Midrash's reading of 'Pharaoh's heart is heavy' as a heart that was a liver.

title.en: The heart of the wise is on his right

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that good middos come from the right chamber and bad ones from the left, and that the wise man's contemplation of Hashem's greatness arouses love of Hashem in the right chamber. He shows this in the order of tefillah, where Birchas Yotzer's contemplation gives birth to the love of Ahavah Rabbah.

title.en: Two kings fighting over the small city

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings 'one nation shall overpower the other' about Yaakov and Esav as the constant war of the yetzer tov and the yetzer hara, and the Tanya's image of the body as a small city two kings fight over. He explains that the Godly soul wants to rule the body alone, with all its limbs, powers and garments subjugated to it.

title.en: Chabad gives birth to love that overflows

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains what the yetzer tov wants: chochmah, binah and daas of the Godly soul filling the mind, giving birth to fear and love like a father and mother give birth to children. The love is to fill the right chamber until it spills into the left and subdues the sitra achra there.

title.en: Matzah with appetite: serving with both inclinations

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Mishnah wants matzah eaten with appetite if a mitzvah should be done only for Hashem's will, and answers that the yetzer hara must serve the yetzer tov. The appetite gives the mitzvah its fire, and this is 'with all your heart, with both your inclinations'.

title.en: Love with delight and avodas matanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the yetzer tov wants the 'evil waters', the drive for pleasure, transformed into love of Hashem, up to love with delight that even simple people taste at high moments such as Shabbos. He distinguishes 'avodas avodah', service by toil, from 'avodas matanah', service as a gift.

title.en: Not a tzaddik gamur; the Zohar's parable

summary.en: Anticipating the next chapter, the Mashgiach explains that only a tzaddik gamur transforms his yetzer hara, while most people's avodah is to subdue it, so no one should despair. He finishes the chapter: the yetzer tov wants thought, speech and action for Hashem alone, the animal soul wants the opposite, yet it too serves man's good, as the Zohar's parable of the king's son and the harlot shows.

catalogTitle: Transforming the Three Weeks

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Three Weeks are great days that have fallen, like the Nephilim, and that the task of these weeks is to lift them up and transform them, and oneself, through Torah, tefillah and emunah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by showing that Zimri was no ordinary sinner but Shlumiel ben Tzurishaddai, a Nasi and one of the seventy souls. From Parshas Shlach on, the parshiyos of Tammuz tell of great people who fell: the meraglim, Korach, Moshe at Mei Merivah, Zimri. The forty days of the meraglim, from Rosh Chodesh Tammuz to Tisha B'Av, are days of midas hadin. The meraglim met the Nephilim, angels cast down from heaven; since the Torah repeats itself in every generation, and Sefer Yetzirah teaches that time parallels place and soul, we meet Nephilim in time: the Three Weeks are lofty days that have fallen, destined to become the greatest festivals. The Mashgiach brings remazim, the Chozeh of Lublin, and the transformations of Lavan into Barzilai and of Balak into the ancestor of Moshiach, and calls on his listeners to dig out the hidden good, transform themselves, and above all daven, as Yehoshua and Kalev did.

en: Zimri was a distinguished tzaddik: Nasi of Shevet Shimon, one of the seventy souls, whose day in Nisan is still marked, and a family was named after him even after his sin.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Tammuz to Tisha B'Av are the days the meraglim spent in Eretz Yisrael, days of midas hadin, and their parshiyos tell of tzaddikim who turned sour.
The Torah is not a history book: what the meraglim met in place, the Nephilim, we meet in time during these forty days.
The Three Weeks are not low days but lofty days that have fallen, destined to become the most joyous days of the year.
The mission of the Three Weeks is to transform them from klala into bracha through extra Torah, tefillah and tzedakah, as Hashem turned Bilaam's curse into a blessing out of love.
Even Lavan, Bilaam and Balak had good at their core, which was later transformed into Barzilai and into Dovid HaMelech and Moshiach.
The missing ingredient by the meraglim was tefillah; Yehoshua and Kalev were saved because they had it.

candidateTopics: time, place and soul in Sefer Yetzirah

title.en: Who was Zimri?

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Pinchas and Zimri and asks who Zimri was. He shows from Chazal that Zimri was Shlumiel ben Tzurishaddai, Nasi of Shevet Shimon and one of the seventy souls who went down to Mitzrayim, whose day in Nisan is still marked by not saying Tachanun, and after whom a family was named even after his sin.

title.en: Tzaddikim who turned sour

summary.en: Contrasting the good guys and bad guys of his childhood stories with the Torah's tzaddikim and resha'im, the Mashgiach says that from Parshas Shlach, read on Shabbos Mevarchim Tammuz, a new figure appears: tzaddikim who fell. He explains that the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Tammuz to Tisha B'Av are the days of the meraglim, days of midas hadin.

title.en: Korach, Mei Merivah and Zimri

summary.en: The Mashgiach follows the pattern through the parshiyos of Tammuz: Korach, the greatest tzaddik of Shevet Levi according to the Zohar, who turned sour; the criticism of Moshe Rabbeinu at Mei Merivah in Chukas; and in Balak and Pinchas, Zimri the Nasi. He asks what is happening in these weeks that tzaddikim fall.

title.en: The meraglim and the Nephilim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the meraglim lost their bitachon when they saw the Nephilim, and identifies the Nephilim of Bereishis as angels who opposed the creation of man, were cast down to earth and brought on the Mabul. He then gives a rule: the Torah is not a history book but repeats itself in every generation and person, so we too meet Nephilim in these forty days.

title.en: Place, time and soul

summary.en: Citing Sefer Yetzirah, the Mashgiach explains that whatever exists in place is found in time and in the soul: the Kodesh HaKodashim in place, Yom Kippur in time and the Kohen Gadol among souls, all meeting on Yom Kippur. Therefore, if there are fallen souls, Nephilim, there are also fallen times.

title.en: The Three Weeks: great days that fell

summary.en: Turning to the Three Weeks, which begin that night, the Mashgiach describes their mourning and asks whether they are really small days. He answers that they are great days which have fallen, destined according to the Navi Zechariah to become the most joyous days when Moshiach comes, and that their fall is felt in the heaviness people find in learning and davening.

title.en: Lifting the days: dig for the treasure

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what to do about the heaviness: not to be pulled down like the generation of the Mabul, but like Noach, Yehoshua and Kalev to strengthen emunah, learning and tefillah and lift the days. He explains Moshe's word 'dig' to the meraglim with the Rama MiPano's reading of 'bikurei anavim': these are days of the Satan, yet one who digs finds the good hidden in them.

title.en: Proofs that these are great days

summary.en: The Mashgiach proves the greatness of these days: Aharon's 'chag laHashem machar' pointed to Shiva Asar B'Tammuz, and the Chasam Sofer calculates that Rus conceived Oved on that day, so the Three Weeks begin with Moshiach and end with him, born on Tisha B'Av according to the Midrash. He adds a remez: 'somech Hashem lechol hanoflim' equals Tammuz in gematria, while Av, which is only bent, matches 'zokef lechol hakefufim'.

title.en: Pinchas and the mission of the Three Weeks

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Parshas Pinchas, read in the weeks of churban, speaks of dividing Eretz Yisrael and lists the korbanos of all the Yamim Tovim, because these days are destined to be holidays, and brings the Chozeh of Lublin that the three Shabbosos of the Three Weeks hold Pesach, Shavuos and Sukkos. The mission is to transform these weeks, as Hashem turned Bilaam's curse into a blessing out of love.

title.en: Lavan, Bilaam, Naval and Barzilai

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from Targum Yonasan that Bilaam was Lavan, and from the Arizal that this soul passed through Bilaam and Naval until it became Barzilai HaGiladi, who did the opposite of Naval for Dovid HaMelech. He asks why so wicked a soul was transformed so fast, and answers that Lavan had good at his core: his children Rachel, Leah, Zilpah and Bilhah and his son-in-law Yaakov, whose initials spell Barzilai.

title.en: Balak's hidden good and the season of transformation

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that even Balak had good within him, since Eglon, father of Rus and ancestor of Dovid HaMelech and Moshiach, came from him. From here he calls this the season of transformation: whoever suspects something bad in himself should turn it to good, for the people of these parshiyos were great people who fell and must get up; then he asks why Kalev and Yehoshua did not fall.

title.en: The kernel of chametz: the missing tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a tzaddik who prepared a perfect Pesach yet found a kernel of wheat in his soup at the Seder; an angel told him in a dream that he had forgotten to daven for a kosher Pesach, and that a bird had dropped the kernel down the chimney. So too Yehoshua was saved by Moshe's tefillah and Kalev by davening at the graves of the Avos, and the Mashgiach closes with a tefillah that the Three Weeks be transformed into sasson and simcha.

catalogTitle: רשע וטוב לו' הטוב כפוף בו' רבבות מדריגות בו. רשע ורע לו. בינוני' הרע בו כמו הטוב אבל הוא אינו עושה רע. ובעיתות 'רצון' הרע הולך לו.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapters 11 and 12, the Mashgiach explains the levels of the rasha v'tov lo and the rasha v'ra lo, and defines the beinoni as one who never sins, whose evil is silenced during proper davening.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens chapter 11 of Tanya: opposite the tzaddik v'ra lo stands the rasha v'tov lo, whose good is bent under the evil in countless levels; the lightest stumbles only rarely, in a little lashon hara, levity or a sinful thought. He explains why hirhurei aveirah are easy to fall into yet graver than a deed, since thought reaches the world of Beriah. He discusses when thought alone is a sin, the rasha who regrets and the three kinds of atonement, and then the rasha v'ra lo, from whom the good has departed yet still surrounds him as a makif, so that he may complete a minyan. In chapter 12 he defines the beinoni as one who never sins though he still has free choice, notes that every Jew can become a beinoni, and explains that during krias shema and tefillah the evil in him is silenced, while afterward it may speak but he does not listen.

en: The rasha v'tov lo still has good within him, but it is bent and suppressed under the evil, and there are countless levels of how much it is suppressed.
Sinful thoughts are light in that even upright people easily stumble in them, but graver than a sin in their damage, since a bad thought blemishes the world of Beriah.
The rasha v'ra lo has driven the good out of himself and never does teshuvah, yet the good still surrounds him as a makif, so he remains a Jew who believes and can complete a minyan.
A beinoni never commits a sin, yet unlike the complete tzaddik he still has free choice; the Tanya, the 'Sefer shel Beinonim', teaches how to be a beinoni, which every Jew can become.
During krias shema and tefillah said properly, the evil in the beinoni is silenced and only the yetzer tov rules; after davening the evil may speak again, but the beinoni does not listen to it.

thought, speech and action and the higher worlds

title.en: The rasha v'tov lo and his levels

summary.en: Recalling the tzaddik v'ra lo of the previous chapter, the Mashgiach reads the opening of chapter 11: the rasha v'tov lo, whose good is bent under the evil in countless levels. The lightest of them falls rarely, in one of the three garments: a little lashon hara or levity in speech, or sinful thoughts.

title.en: Why sinful thoughts are light yet severe

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the 'light' rasha who has not yet done teshuvah, and explains the two sides of hirhurei aveirah: they are easy to fall into, even for upright people, yet worse than a sin. He maps action, speech and thought onto the worlds of Asiyah, Yetzirah and Beriah, so a bad thought blemishes as high as the Throne of Glory.

title.en: When thought alone is a sin; regret and atonement

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a bad thought is generally not joined to the deed, except in heresy and immorality, where the thought itself is the sin. Even an upright Jew who stumbles in such things is called a rasha at that moment, but afterward the good in him regrets and he seeks forgiveness; the Mashgiach lists the three kinds of atonement.

title.en: The rasha v'ra lo: the good surrounds him

summary.en: The Mashgiach moves to one who often falls into grave sins yet still has regrets, still a rasha v'tov lo, and then to the rasha v'ra lo, who never does teshuvah because the good has departed from within him. Even so he believes in the Ribono shel Olam and would give his life rather than serve idols, because the good stands around him as a makif, as if waiting at the door.

title.en: Counting him for a minyan

summary.en: As an example the Mashgiach explains that such a person may be counted for a minyan, and explains what a minyan is: ten souls join into one and draw down a holiness that nine tzaddikim cannot. He asks how one whose good has left can join, answers that the kedushah stays around him as a makif, and reads the closing lines of chapter 11 with the saying that wherever ten are gathered the Shechinah rests.

title.en: Who is a beinoni

summary.en: Opening chapter 12, the Mashgiach defines the beinoni as one who never sins yet still has free choice, which answers how Rabbah could think he was a beinoni. He notes the title 'Sefer shel Beinonim': the Ba'al HaTanya cannot make anyone a tzaddik, but every Jew can become a beinoni. 'Never sinned and never will' refers to his present state, as even great people like the meraglim and Korach fell.

title.en: Krias shema and tefillah as a time of gadlus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the ten powers of the beinoni's G-dly soul do not rule alone, yet at special times the evil has no say: during krias shema and tefillah, a time of gadlus hamochin when a Jew rises to higher worlds where there is no evil. Then he awakens the love of Hashem in the right chamber of his heart and fulfills the mitzvah of loving Hashem.

title.en: Preparing to daven; the two judges

summary.en: The Mashgiach walks through the preparation from waking up through pesukei dezimra, birchas yotzer, ahavah rabbah and shema, which brings a time when the yetzer hara is silenced. He compares the beinoni to a court with two judges who listens only to the good one, and stresses that this is only with proper davening, not a rushed one; after davening the evil may speak again, but the beinoni does not heed it.

catalogTitle: בינוני מוח שליט על הלב' היצה"ר אינו מתלבש בלבוש מחשבה דיבור או מעשה אבל הוא במציאות אצלו.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 12, the Mashgiach explains that in the beinoni the evil inclination is still present but can never clothe itself in thought, speech or deed, because the mind rules over the heart.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach recalls the question from chapter one, how Rabbah could call himself a beinoni, and how the earlier chapters defined the tzaddik; the beinoni never sins yet still desires evil, so in essence he is not called a tzaddik. Chapter 12 explains that his evil never gains enough strength to clothe itself in his body; he may even have once been wicked and done teshuvah. Using the Tanya's parable of two kings fighting over a small city, the Mashgiach explains the exception of Shema and tefillah, and expands on davening as passage through the heavenly chambers, where foreign thoughts mean being pushed out, and on preparing with teshuvah and joining oneself to all Jews. The evil inclination stays a mere passer-by, never a guest or master, because the mind rules the heart. He adds that rare situations can exist where a person truly cannot help himself, but one must always suspect that he can. A bad thought is driven out by holy thoughts, as light drives away darkness. Finally, even after davening the yetzer suggests things, and the impression of davening and the hidden love keep the beinoni in control.

en: The beinoni never sins, but because he still has a desire for evil he is not called a tzaddik in essence, only in judgment.
In the beinoni the evil never becomes strong enough to clothe itself in the body through thought, speech or deed.
During Shema and tefillah, when the mind is in a state of greatness, the evil in the beinoni has no dominion at all; afterwards it reawakens.
The mind rules over the heart by the nature of man's creation, so a person can always overcome his yetzer and cannot claim he was unable to help it.
A bad thought is best driven away by thinking of holy matters, just as a little light drives away much darkness.
Even after davening the yetzer still sits in its place and makes suggestions; the impression of the davening and the hidden love keep the beinoni in control.

title.en: Rabbah's question and the tzaddik defined

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the question from chapter one, how Rabbah, who served Hashem every moment, could call himself a beinoni, and reviews the complete tzaddik who has killed his evil inclination. He explains that the beinoni never sins, yet since he still desires evil he is a tzaddik only in judgment, not in essence.

title.en: The evil cannot clothe itself in the body

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of Tanya chapter 12: in the beinoni the evil never gains enough strength to clothe itself in thought, speech or deed. He adds that one may become a beinoni after teshuvah, and recalls the parable of two kings fighting over a small city, where the good king holds his position, except during Shema and tefillah.

title.en: Davening as passage through the heichalos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains, in the name of the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Chasam Sofer, that every word of Torah and tefillah is a heavenly chamber, and davening ascends through the worlds. Foreign thoughts during davening mean the keruvim are pushing a person out, so before davening one does teshuvah and includes oneself with the tzaddikim and all Jews; davening, especially Shacharis, is a war, with tallis and tefillin as its weapons.

title.en: The beinoni during and after davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the beinoni is always armed for the war, so during Shema and tefillah the other king has no permission to enter; the Tanya describes this as the time of greatness of mind, contemplating Hashem's greatness in the blessings before Shema. After davening the evil reawakens, but since it is only one of two judges and the good also sits, it cannot bring its desire into action.

title.en: Passer-by, guest, master; the mind rules the heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the yetzer has three names, a passer-by, a guest and a master of the house, and says that in the beinoni it always remains a passer-by who is turned away at the door. The reason, from the Ra'aya Mehemna, is that the mind by nature rules over the heart, so no one can say his yetzer overpowered him.

title.en: Rare cases where one cannot help himself

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds, noting that this is not in the Tanya, that occasionally Hashem places a person in a situation where he truly cannot control himself and is not responsible; but this is rare, and a person must always suspect that he can help himself. In general the mind rules the heart, and the beinoni says no to every suggestion and pushes the thought away.

title.en: Light drives away darkness

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a bad thought is driven away more easily by thinking of holy matters, bringing the passuk in Koheles about the advantage of wisdom over folly like light over darkness. Darkness, he says, is a real creation, as the passuk in Yeshayahu says, yet a little light pushes away much darkness; so the folly of the kelipah is pushed away by the holy thought, and even so the beinoni is not called a tzaddik.

title.en: The yetzer still present; three daily failings

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the yetzer still sits on its bench, and after davening the love of Hashem is only hidden, so the yetzer can make suggestions, even of forbidden things, which the beinoni rejects. He brings the Gemara that no one escapes hirhur aveirah and iyun tefillah daily, with Tosafos' reading of iyun tefillah as feeling one has davened well, and concludes that the impression of davening and the hidden love keep the yetzer from ruling.

catalogTitle: בינוני - זה וזה שופטן וה' מכריע. תשובה על הקושיא על המילים - תהא בעיניך כרשע.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why the beinoni is judged by two 'judges', the good and evil inclinations, with Hashem as the deciding voice, and how this answers why even a tzaddik should regard himself as a rasha.

abstract.en: Finishing Tanya chapter 12, the Mashgiach explains that the beinoni cannot stop thoughts of envy, hatred or resentment from arising, but has the choice not to accept them. Emunah that everything comes from Hashem removes resentment, as David said of Shimi ben Gera and as Yosef repaid his brothers with good; a tzaddik told a shopkeeper to thank Hashem for every customer who went to his competitor. Moving to chapter 13, he explains the Gemara's 'zeh v'zeh shoftan': the yetzer hara is a judge giving an opinion, not a ruler, and Hashem is the decider who helps the good side. The world is balanced between good and evil, but the Creator stands above it, as light drives out darkness. Hashem helps only one who struggles himself. This answers 'be in your eyes like a rasha': without Hashem's help the yetzer would win. Finally, the beinoni's evil is only asleep during prayer, which explains Rabbah's error in calling himself a beinoni.

en: The beinoni cannot prevent bad thoughts from arising, but he has the choice not to accept them willingly and to push them out at once.
Resentment toward someone who caused harm contradicts emunah, since everything that happens to a person is decreed from Heaven and the other person is only the stick.
The yetzer hara in the beinoni is a judge who states his opinion, not a ruler who must be obeyed, and the halachah follows the decider, Hashem, who helps the yetzer tov.
Hashem's help comes only to one who struggles against the yetzer hara himself, like the mitzvah to help unload an animal only together with its owner.
'Be in your eyes like a rasha' means that even one who does no sin should know that the yetzer in him is as strong as in a rasha, and only Hashem's help keeps him from falling.
During Krias Shema and tefillah the beinoni's evil is only asleep, subdued but not transformed, and it can wake up again afterwards.

title.en: The beinoni's choice over passing thoughts

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains from Tanya chapter 12 that thoughts of envy, hatred and resentment come to the beinoni on their own, but he can refuse to accept them and push them away. He adds that resentment toward another Jew goes against emunah, since whatever happens is decreed from Heaven.

title.en: Shimi, Yosef and the competing shop

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings David HaMelech's response to Shimi ben Gera, the mashal of the dog that bites the stick, and Yosef repaying his brothers with good. He then tells of a tzaddik who told a man to thank Hashem each time a customer entered his competitor's shop, until the thanks became true in his heart.

title.en: Two judges and the One who decides

summary.en: Starting chapter 13, the Mashgiach explains the Gemara's 'zeh v'zeh shoftan' from the plural 'shoftei nafsho': the yetzer hara is like a judge voicing an opinion from the heart, not a ruler, and the yetzer tov argues against it. The halachah follows the decider, Hashem, as the Gemara says that without His help one could not overcome the yetzer.

title.en: A balanced world and the light that drives out darkness

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a teaching of the Maggid Meisharim that Hashem is the decider who helps the tzaddik, who still receives full credit at the judgment. He explains that the world's good and evil are balanced, as the Gemara shows from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya, but the Creator stands above the balance, just as light does not mix with darkness but drives it out.

title.en: Then how can anyone sin?

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks: if Hashem always sides with the good, how can a person ever sin? He answers from the mitzvah of 'azov ta'azov imo', which applies only when the owner works along: Hashem helps only one who struggles against the yetzer hara himself, and so the beinoni who fights never sins.

title.en: Answering 'be in your eyes like a rasha'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem's help is the light of Hashem in the G-dly soul, which pushes away the darkness, as Yosef was helped when he could no longer resist. With this he answers the question from Tanya's first chapter: the tzaddik should see himself like a rasha because the yetzer in him is just as strong, and only Hashem's help keeps him from sinning.

title.en: The yetzer hara is not gone, only quiet

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the beinoni's evil keeps its full strength, and every physical act strengthens it further. Only during Krias Shema and tefillah, or for one who learns Torah lishmah all day, does the yetzer have no voice, yet even then it is not driven out but only asleep.

title.en: Subdued, not transformed: Rabbah's error

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that even in prayer the G-dly soul only rules over the animal soul like a wrestler on top, which is iskafya rather than transformation; only a tzaddik like David HaMelech, whose heart was 'chalal', has killed the evil. This answers Tanya's question of how Rabbah could call himself a beinoni: his whole day of learning was like the time of Krias Shema.

catalogTitle: The Hidden חסד of the חורבן

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chodesh Av carries the mercy of a Father, since the Churban fell on wood and stone to save Klal Yisrael, and he shows why Esav's showy kibud av outdoes Yaakov's and lets him prevail in Av.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Chodesh Av, a month of mourning that will be turned to joy, and with the Maharal: the curses run backwards, from vav to hey, so they are only temporary. He links Tammuz and Av to Reuven and Shimon. Then he brings Avimi, who honored his father perfectly and was helped to explain why the psalm of the Churban is called a song: Hashem poured His anger on wood and stone and saved the people. Kibud av awakens the mercy of the Father above, and the name Av itself means that Hashem punishes as a father. The Mashgiach then asks why Esav outdid Yaakov in kibud av and so prevails in Av. Esav's honor is external, a veneer driven by the Satan, like the goy of Ashkelon who did not know his true father. Kibud av and love of Eretz Yisrael share one root, and together with tzedakah they build the Beis HaMikdash.

en: The curses of Bechukosai run from vav to hey, against the order of the alphabet, which shows, as the Maharal explains, that they are a passing state that will turn into blessing.
The Churban was an act of a Father's mercy: Hashem poured His anger on the wood and stones of the Beis HaMikdash so that Klal Yisrael would survive, which is why Asaf calls the psalm a song.
Honoring parents awakens above the conduct of Hashem as our Father, who has mercy on His children.
The name of the month, Av, tells that Hashem punishes like a father, with mercy and to set the son straight, so Av is a month of consolation.
Esav's kibud av surpasses Yaakov's only on the outside; inwardly he wished his father dead, and the Mashgiach says the Satan drives the nations' devotion to this mitzvah.
Kibud av and the longing for Eretz Yisrael share one root, since both come from a person's origin, and kibud av and tzedakah are the two mitzvos that build the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Av, and curses that run backwards

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the coming of Chodesh Av, an unwelcome month of mourning, and the hope that its fast will become a day of joy. He brings the Midrash that the blessings run from aleph to tav while the curses run backwards from vav to hey, and the Maharal's explanation that the curses are outside Hashem's plan and only temporary.

title.en: Tammuz is Reuven, Av is Shimon

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that Reuven, fourth in the camps and among the nesi'im, corresponds to Tammuz, which is why the three weeks begin around Korach and Dasan and Aviram. Shimon, fifth, corresponds to Av, and in Pinchas we read of Zimri, the nasi of Shimon.

title.en: Avimi and the song of Asaf

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara about Avimi, who stood bent over his sleeping father holding water, and in that merit explained why Asaf calls his psalm on the Churban a song and not a lament. Hashem transferred the punishment from Klal Yisrael to the wood and stones of the Beis HaMikdash, and the people were saved.

title.en: Kibud av awakens the Father above

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every mitzvah awakens something corresponding above, and honoring parents switches on Hashem's conduct as a merciful Father. He asks why, then, Hashem seems not to act as a Father in a long golus, and answers from Avimi: the Churban itself came from a Father's mercy.

title.en: The name Av and the comfort it brings

summary.en: Following the Maharal's rule that a name reveals one's mission, the Mashgiach shows that Avimi spells 'days of Av' and his father Avuha holds hey before vav, the curses in reverse. Av means Hashem punishes as a father, so one weeps but not too much, and the month will become one of joy.

title.en: Esav's kibud av and his hold on Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the nations seem more devoted to kibud av than Jews, and that Yaakov feared Esav for his kibud av and his living in Eretz Yisrael. Av, the month of the Father, is Esav's month of success, when he destroyed the Beis HaMikdash twice; yet Esav's honor was external, since he hoped for his father's death in order to kill Yaakov.

title.en: The Satan behind the goy's kibud av

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a great rav in Poland who as a child told his father that the same Satan that sends the goyish boys to school keeps him in bed, and suggests the Satan drives Esav's excellence in kibud av. He brings the Gemara of Dama ben Nesina and the Chida that Hashem is a King to the nations but a Father only to Yidden.

title.en: Fine clothes and third-person speech

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who said Esav outdid him by serving his father in special garments, and the Ksav Sofer, who notes that Esav spoke to Yitzchak in the third person like a subject to a king while Yaakov spoke simply. A son at home needs no veneer because of the love between them; Esav shows off his kibud av like the chazir shows its split hooves.

title.en: Why both examples come from Ashkelon

summary.en: The Mashgiach argues that a loving Jewish father would be upset had his son lost a fortune rather than wake him, so Dama ben Nesina's conduct reflects a king and subject, not intimacy. He asks why the Gemara names Ashkelon, and explains that the Pelishtim there descended from swapped wives and lacked the natural bond to a father, so their kibud av is only external.

title.en: Kibud av and Eretz Yisrael share one root

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one honors parents because they are one's origin, and a Jew longs for Eretz Yisrael because Adam was formed from its earth, from the place of the Beis HaMikdash and the mizbeiach. So the reward of kibud av is long days in the land. He brings the Maharal that the nations honor parents more because their whole world is the body their parents gave them, while a Jew's neshamah existed before.

title.en: What the Gemara's question really asks

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how a goy of Ashkelon could teach the measure of kibud av, and rereads the Gemara: it asks how great this mitzvah is, and answers that the Satan drives the goyim to it because kibud av holds the building of the Beis HaMikdash and the end of golus. He compares tzedakah, which also builds the Beis HaMikdash, citing the Gemara on not taking tzedakah from a goy and Daniel's punishment for advising Nevuchadnetzar to give tzedakah.

title.en: The Torah as Father; welcoming Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach extends kibud av to a teacher and to the Torah itself, which one should learn with respect as Hashem's Torah. He closes that Av is welcomed with bitachon and emunah, that Zimri will also have his tikkun, and that Tammuz and Menachem Av equal Melech HaMashiach in gematria.

catalogTitle: יש כמה מדריגות במדריגת אמת. הדרכה וי"ד שלא להיות עצוב כשבאים אצלו מחשבות רעות ועצה איך להתחזק כנגדם.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that truth has many levels, so the beinoni's prayer is true by his own measure, and that a beinoni should not be saddened by bad thoughts but fight them through the hidden love every Jew has for Hashem.

abstract.en: Continuing Tanya chapter 13, the Mashgiach explains why a beinoni's love in prayer is not called 'avodas emes' compared to tzaddikim: truth is lasting, as 'sfas emes tikon la'ad', and a fervor that gives way to desire after davening shows it lacked truth. Yet truth has levels. Yaakov, the attribute of truth, is the middle bar running through all the boards of the Mishkan, each board a level of Jews, so what is falsehood for a higher person is truth for a lower one. He brings the Yismach Moshe's answer to the Rema: every Jew has his own reading of the Torah by his level. Moving to chapter 14, he teaches that a beinoni must not feel bad about bad thoughts; he should rejoice at the chance to fulfil 'lo sasuru', strengthen himself with the hidden love that makes even simple Jews give their lives, and fight every sin.

en: Truth is what endures: a tzaddik's fervor in prayer that gives way to desire for this world afterward shows that it lacked truth.
Truth has levels: what would be falsehood for a higher person is true service for a lower one, according to his level.
Every Jew has his own reading of the Torah according to his level, as the Yismach Moshe answers the question on the Rema.
A beinoni should not feel bad when bad thoughts come to him even after good preparation for davening; this is how he was created and his mission in the world.
When a bad thought comes he should rejoice, since pushing it away fulfils the mitzvah of 'lo sasuru' and breaks the sitra achra.
Every Jew, even the worst, has a hidden love for Hashem that would make him give his life rather than serve idols; he sins only because a spirit of folly makes him forget it.

title.en: Why the beinoni's prayer is not called truth

summary.en: Continuing Tanya chapter 13, the Mashgiach explains that the beinoni subdues evil only during prayer, and that relative to tzaddikim this is not 'avodas emes'. Truth, he explains from 'sfas emes tikon la'ad', is lasting, while falsehood and the pleasures of this world are momentary and leave a person empty.

title.en: Yaakov, the middle bar of the Mishkan

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yaakov, the attribute of tiferes, is the middle bar that runs from end to end through the boards of the Mishkan, each board being a level among Jews. He reads the names Yisrael and Yaakov as spanning head to heel, and brings the Yerushalmi that the boards had a fixed order, marked by writing, which may not be changed.

title.en: Each level has its own truth

summary.en: Since Yaakov's attribute of truth passes through every board, the Mashgiach concludes that each Jew has his own level of truth. For a tzaddik, desire returning after prayer shows the prayer was falsehood; for a beinoni, being cleaved to Hashem during prayer alone is the truth of his level, as the Tanya says.

title.en: Every Jew's own reading of the Torah

summary.en: From 'darosh darash', the middle of the Torah in the week's parsha, the Mashgiach learns that every Jew has his own interpretation of the Torah by his level. He illustrates it with the Rema that one who is 'mafleg bachasidus' may give his life even for other mitzvos, and the Yismach Moshe's answer to how this fits 'vachai bahem'.

title.en: Two readings of 'sfas emes tikon la'ad'

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies this to the passuk 'sfas emes tikon la'ad': for the great tzaddik it means truth that never fades, while for the beinoni it means truth that is stored away until his next prayer. He reads the Tanya's words that the attribute of truth is Yaakov's, the middle bar and a 'heritage without bounds', reaching every level, and illustrates with how a twelve-hour learning day is judged differently for the Chofetz Chaim and for a young bochur.

title.en: Chapter 14: the beinoni and free choice

summary.en: Having finished the Tanya's foundations, the Mashgiach begins chapter 14: the beinoni never acts on the yetzer hara's words though he hears them, and he should not feel bad that bad thoughts come after davening, since this is how he was created. Being repulsed by evil is not always in a person's power, but his thought, speech and action always are.

title.en: Rejoicing at the mitzvah of 'lo sasuru'

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that the first bad thought is not in a person's control and he need not feel bad about it; on the contrary, he should rejoice, since pushing it out fulfils 'lo sasuru acharei levavchem', one of the greatest mitzvos, which breaks the sitra achra. He then reads the Tanya's declaration that one does not want to be separated from Hashem but to cleave to Him with thought, speech and action.

title.en: The hidden love and the spirit of folly

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the hidden love, mentioned here for the first time in the Tanya: every Jew, even a wicked one, has it, and at a time of decree to serve idols simple Jews gave their lives. He asks why such a Jew commits other sins, and answers with the Tanya that a spirit of folly makes him think other sins do not cut him off, so the beinoni resolves to fight the yetzer hara over every sin.

title.en: Love with delight, and the beinoni's work

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that truly despising evil comes only from 'ahavah betaanugim', which the tzaddik has constantly and the beinoni only at moments, especially on Shabbos and Yom Tov, a gift like 'avodas matanah'. When it is absent, desire for this world fills the void; this answers the question of Iyov 'You created tzaddikim', and the beinoni's work is never to obey the yetzer hara.

catalogTitle: חילוקים בבינונים - עובד ה' ואשר לא עבדו.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's distinction between the beinoni who serves Hashem by constant battle and the beinoni who 'does not serve Him' because his learning comes easily, and shows that real avodah means going beyond one's nature and habit.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by stressing that every beinoni is sent a battle suited to his nature, health, family and surroundings, as Avraham Avinu, born to Terach, had to fight against everything he came from. He then reads the Tanya on the passuk in Malachi that distinguishes between tzaddik and rasha, and between one who serves G-d and one who does not. 'Oved' is present tense: the beinoni is in an ongoing war, while the tzaddik bears the name as a title. The one who 'does not serve' is also a beinoni and never sins, yet wages no war, because he is a masmid by nature or because hidden love inherited from the Avos suffices for him. A masmid by habit was an oved while he worked, but becomes one who does not serve once it is easy. Using the Gemara's 100 versus 101 reviews and the donkey-drivers' mashal, the Mashgiach defines avodah as going beyond habit, through contemplating Hashem's greatness or awakening the hidden love.

en: Each person is given his own battle according to his nature and circumstances, and he should not envy another's soul.
The beinoni is called 'oved Elokim' because he is constantly at war with his yetzer hara, while the tzaddik carries the name as a title.
The one who 'does not serve' is not a rasha; he is a beinoni who never sins, even through bittul Torah, but has no battle to fight.
Whether a person is a masmid by nature or became one through habit, as long as he only does what comes easily he is called 'lo avado'.
Avodah means doing more than one's habit, as the Gemara contrasts reviewing a chapter 100 times with 101 times.
There are two ways to break one's nature: contemplating the greatness of Hashem, or awakening the hidden love in the heart.
