title.en: Every beinoni has his own battle

summary.en: Continuing from the previous chapter, the Mashgiach says the beinoni's war never ends and each one is sent a battle suited to his nature, health, family and surroundings. He brings Avraham Avinu, born to Terach, who had to fight everything he came from, and says one should not envy another's soul.

title.en: Tzaddik and oved Elokim

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya on the passuk in Malachi and asks how 'tzaddik' and 'oved Elokim' differ. 'Oved' is present tense: the beinoni is still fighting, and with the mashal of a swimmer he shows that toil can feel like pleasure; for the tzaddik, 'oved' is a settled title, since he has already driven out his yetzer hara.

title.en: The beinoni who 'does not serve'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the beinoni has two levels, and the one 'who does not serve' is not a rasha, since he never sins, not even bittul Torah. He is called so because he wages no war: learning and davening come easily to him, perhaps because he was born and raised in holiness, while one who struggles with every sugya earns far more reward.

title.en: The natural masmid and hidden love

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the 'lo avado' needs no battle: he is a masmid by nature, with a calm temperament that does not crave the world's excitements, so he need not contemplate Hashem's greatness to overcome his yetzer hara. The hidden love that every Jew has suffices for him, but he makes no effort to become better than he is.

title.en: Avraham Avinu, a new creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the hidden love is an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, whose toil on himself made him a new creation. He brings 'behibaram' read as 'be-Avraham' and the verses said daily in davening, and explains that Avraham is the source of every Jew's love of Hashem and Yitzchak of his fear.

title.en: The masmid by habit; 100 and 101

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who trained himself to be a masmid, with fines and other means, was an oved Hashem while he struggled, but once it became second nature he is 'lo avado'. Such a person can become an oved by learning more than his habit, with more depth, as the Gemara contrasts reviewing 100 times with 101.

title.en: The donkey drivers and the limit

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Gemara's mashal of the donkey drivers, who charge double for going past their regular limit, compares it to taxi fares, and concludes that the hardest thing is to act against one's habit. He cites Rabbi Yisrael that a masmid is one who holds on past the point where it is hard, and explains that forgetting comes from the sitra achra, whose name Samech-Mem equals 100.

title.en: Going beyond habit: two ways

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a masmid by nature keeps his fixed schedule but will not learn a minute past mealtime; the oved does more than his habit. Reviewing a 101st time brings one into the realm of Michael, whose name equals 101, and the Mashgiach concludes that nature is broken either by contemplating Hashem's greatness or by fanning the hidden love inherited from Avraham Avinu.

catalogTitle: הבינוני יכול להיות כצדיק בעיתות רצון' עיבור נשמת צדיק בתוכו' כשעושה עצמו שמח בטוב ומואס ברע זוכה שזה נעשה טבעו.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains how a beinoni, who cannot choose to be a true tzaddik, can still fulfill the oath 'be a tzaddik': through moments of real joy in Hashem, through habit that becomes second nature, and through the soul of a tzaddik that comes into him (ibbur).

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the Tanya's distinction: a beinoni wages a constant war with the yetzer hara and every Jew can reach that, but being a tzaddik needs a special soul. This explains the double oath, 'be a tzaddik and do not be a rasha': not being a rasha is in everyone's hands, while 'be a tzaddik' means to strive for it. Still, the Tanya says, a person should set times to contemplate that worldly pleasures are worthless and to rejoice in Hashem; even if passing, at his level it counts. Habit also becomes second nature, as with a brachah said with thought. With the parable of Dovid's harp and a tuned piano string he shows that joy below arouses joy above. Perhaps a spark of a tzaddik's soul will come into him, as in the story of Rav Chaim Vital. A Jew's small mitzvah is multiplied above, which he illustrates with Haman and the omer.

en: Being a beinoni, who never sins though the yetzer hara still fights him, is within every Jew's choice; being a tzaddik is not, since it needs a special soul.
This explains why the oath is doubled: 'do not be a rasha' is an absolute obligation, while 'be a tzaddik' means to strive toward it.
Moments of joy in Hashem that a beinoni reaches through contemplation are not absolute truth, yet relative to his level he fulfills 'be a tzaddik' through them.
Habit rules a person and becomes second nature, so repeated contemplation can make loathing evil and rejoicing in Hashem his nature.
A Jew's joy in serving Hashem below arouses a matching joy above, like two strings tuned to the same note.
Through his own effort the beinoni may merit that the soul of a tzaddik enters him (ibbur), and with its help he serves Hashem with true joy.
A Jew's small mitzvah is multiplied as it rises through the worlds, unlike the deeds of a non-Jew, which stay below.

title.en: Why the oath is doubled

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the difference between a tzaddik, who needs a special soul, and a beinoni, whose constant war with the yetzer hara is in every Jew's hands. He uses it to explain the double oath 'be a tzaddik and do not be a rasha', and notes that a Jew can taste joy in Hashem on Shabbos, Yom Tov or during learning, though it does not last.

title.en: Contemplation and habit as second nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's 'nevertheless': a person should set times to contemplate that worldly pleasures are worthless and to rejoice in Hashem. Even if this is not absolute truth for a beinoni, at his level he fulfills 'be a tzaddik'; and since habit becomes second nature, the feeling can become truly his.

title.en: A brachah and learning said with thought

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives examples of building the habit: pausing a few seconds before a brachah to think for Whom and why one makes it, and before learning to think that Torah is the wisdom of Hashem. Done regularly, this becomes nature, and an awakening below brings an awakening above.

title.en: Dovid's harp and the tuned string

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that a harp hung over Dovid's bed and played at midnight, and explains it with a piano tuner's fork: a string tuned to the same note vibrates by itself. Dovid was tuned to Gan Eden; likewise a Jew who rejoices in Hashem arouses Hashem's joy in him, as in 'yismach Yisrael' and 'yismach Hashem'.

title.en: Gilgul, ibbur and Rav Chaim Vital's story

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a soul which failed through negligence to fulfill mitzvos returns in a full gilgul, while one that missed a mitzvah not by its fault, or a lofty soul that longs for mitzvos, comes into a living Jew for a while as an ibbur and helps him do the mitzvah. He describes unexplained times of great love and closeness as such an ibbur, and tells how Rav Chaim Vital sat on the grave of Benayahu ben Yehoyada and the Arizal stood up for him.

title.en: A tzaddik's soul enters him; the sundial

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the Tanya: one who accustoms himself to rejoice in Hashem will play the music of joy on his soul, and perhaps a spirit from above, a spark of a tzaddik's soul, will come into him so that he serves with true joy. This is a third way to fulfill 'be a tzaddik', and the joy he causes above is far greater than what he feels, like a sundial's shadow moving an inch while the sun moves millions of miles.

title.en: Haman's ten thousand talents and the omer

summary.en: The Mashgiach repeats a thought he said at the Pesach seudah: the Gemara tells that Haman found Mordechai teaching the laws of the omer's handful and said it outweighed his ten thousand talents. He explains that a Jew's mitzvah rises and is multiplied through the worlds while a non-Jew's deed stays below, and he distinguishes 'aseres' (a collective, a multiplication) from 'isaron' (a division, as in 'ishon', a small person in the eye).

title.en: The barley omer is lifted up

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the omer, brought of barley, animal food, like the minchas sotah, is the cheapest offering, yet it is called the omer of waving because it is lifted up and turns from animal into man, raising the Jews day by day until Shavuos. He concludes that the beinoni's small joy below arouses great joy above, and with the help of the soul that comes into him he fulfills 'be a tzaddik' in truth.

catalogTitle: Understanding the מועד of 'ט באב and the יו”ט of ט”ו באב

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tisha B'Av is truly a mo'ed rooted in Pesach, Shabbos and Shemini Atzeres, destined to become a Yom Tov, and that Tu B'Av is the Yom Tov of the ba'al teshuvah who rises from the grave.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Mishnah's term 'the week in which Tisha B'Av falls' and asks why Shabbos, the day of blessing, ushers in the aveilus, and why Tisha B'Av is called a mo'ed on which Tachanun is not said. He shows that Pesach fixes the weekday of Tisha B'Av and that the beitzah on the Seder plate plants it, because there is no absolute destruction for Klal Yisrael: Tisha B'Av is rooted in geulah, Moshiach is born on it, and every aveilus, even a private one, draws its laws from Yom Tov. He explains why Shabbos Chazon is the greatest Shabbos and why the meal before Tisha B'Av on Shabbos is like Shlomo's feast, through the Arizal's teaching that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, whose day is Shemini Atzeres. Through the three dimensions of place, time and soul he explains the mo'ed of Tisha B'Av, and he ends with the Jew lying in his grave, whose Yom Tov is Tu B'Av, the day of the ba'al teshuvah.

en: The aveilus of Tisha B'Av week begins only from the Shabbos before it, so Shabbos, the day of blessing, is what ushers in the aveilus.
Tisha B'Av is a mo'ed, a time of meeting with Hashem, which is why Tachanun is not said on it.
The first day of Pesach fixes the weekday of Tisha B'Av because Tisha B'Av is rooted in the day of geulah and is destined to become a Yom Tov.
There is no absolute destruction or absolute evil for Klal Yisrael; every aveilus is only a veil over something good, as the law of seven days of mourning is learned from the Yom Tov.
Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, so Tisha B'Av is in a sense a gilgul of Shemini Atzeres, Shlomo's day, and will turn back into it.
Every mo'ed carries a blessing to take home; the blessing of Tisha B'Av is the knowledge that Hashem is with Klal Yisrael even in churban.
Tu B'Av is the Yom Tov of the ba'al teshuvah who leaves his grave, and so it is greater than Pesach, Shavuos and Sukkos.

title.en: Why Shabbos ushers in the aveilus

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the laws of the week of Tisha B'Av depend on the Shabbos before it, and asks why the Shabbos of blessing should usher in aveilus. He then asks why Tisha B'Av is called a mo'ed, a meeting, so that Tachanun is not said on it.

title.en: Pesach sets the day of Tisha B'Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Pesach and Tisha B'Av as two extremes, and shows that Pesach, the head of the festivals, fixes the weekday of Tisha B'Av. He answers that Tisha B'Av is rooted in the day of geulah, is destined to become a day of simcha, and is the day Moshiach is born.

title.en: The beitzah and a passing churban

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the beitzah on the Seder plate plants Tisha B'Av in Pesach and is the remedy for Amalek, who brought about Tisha B'Av. Tisha B'Av is a passing condition, and Pesach gives it the first place among the Yamim Tovim.

title.en: Shabbos and the bittersweet aveilus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the week is Hashem's own calendar and its special day is Shabbos, so no aveilus can begin without Shabbos; the aveilus of Tisha B'Av is full of nechamah and hope. He brings the Gemara deriving seven days of mourning from Yom Tov to show that even a private aveilus is only a veil.

title.en: Shabbos Chazon, the greatest Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Shabbos Chazon is called the greatest Shabbos of the year, and that its haftarah is from Yeshayahu, the navi of geulah, not Yirmiyahu, the navi of churban. He suggests that 'Chazon' points to the heart, which senses the geulah hidden under the aveilus.

title.en: Tefillin at Minchah and Shlomo's feast

summary.en: The Mashgiach suggests that tefillin are not worn on Tisha B'Av morning because we still hope it will become a Yom Tov. He then contrasts the poor seudah hamafsekes with the Gemara's rule that when Tisha B'Av follows Shabbos one eats a meal like Shlomo's feast in his time.

title.en: Yirmiyahu, gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal's teaching that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, who returned to see the destruction of the Beis HaMikdash he built. Each tzaddik has his day: Tisha B'Av is Yirmiyahu's, Shemini Atzeres is Shlomo's, a sample of the days of Moshiach when the moon was full.

title.en: Tisha B'Av, a gilgul of Shemini Atzeres

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that no person ever reached complete fulfillment except Shlomo HaMelech, a sample of the days of Moshiach. When Shlomo returned as Yirmiyahu his day became Tisha B'Av, so Tisha B'Av is a gilgul of Shemini Atzeres and will change back; this is why the meal before it on Shabbos is like Shlomo in his time.

title.en: Why Tu B'Av is the greatest Yom Tov

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah that there were no Yamim Tovim like Tu B'Av and Yom Kippur, and the Gemara's account of the generation of the desert dying every Tisha B'Av until the decree stopped. He asks why that should make Tu B'Av greater than Pesach, Shavuos and Sukkos.

title.en: Place, time and soul: the mo'ed

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Sefer Yetzirah's three dimensions of place, time and soul, which meet on Yom Kippur in the Kodesh HaKodashim through the Kohen Gadol. A mo'ed is a meeting with Hashem from which one takes home a blessing, and the blessing of Tisha B'Av is that Hashem sits with Klal Yisrael on the ground.

title.en: Souls that are Shabbos and Yom Tov

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that time is duplicated in soul: a talmid chacham is called Shabbos, and the one who supports him receives blessing from him as one receives from Shabbos. Lesser souls who work but are bound to Torah are Yom Tov, and others are a mo'ed.

title.en: The Tisha B'Av Jew and Tu B'Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the gifted Jew who could have been great but lies in his grave thinking it is life; he is a Tisha B'Av, yet we do not despair, since no Jew is lost forever. When he leaves the grave and does teshuvah, his Yom Tov is Tu B'Av, greater than all the festivals, as a ba'al teshuvah is greater than a tzaddik.

title.en: Dancing in the vineyards; the gold will shine

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the daughters of Yisrael dancing on Tu B'Av as those who came out of the grave, and calls on those still in it to join them. He compares the meal before Tisha B'Av on Shabbos to the Ran's explanation of the meal of Erev Yom Kippur, and closes with the hope that the tarnished gold will be polished and Tu B'Av will become the Yom Tov of the world.

catalogTitle: עבודת הבינוני - לידע שנברא לעבודת ה'' ושלא לעשות רע. כל יהודי לפי שורש נשמתו.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 16 the Mashgiach explains that a beinoni who cannot feel love of Hashem must at least know it with his mind, and, by way of the dispute between Chabad and the Polish tzaddikim, that every Jew serves Hashem according to the root of his soul, like a letter in its exact place in the Sefer Torah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter 16: the beinoni cannot rule his heart, so he must at least know with his mind that he was created to serve Hashem. A tzaddik feels love of Hashem; the beinoni is given a taste only at times of favor, such as Shabbos and Yom Tov. Since love and fear are the wings of every mitzvah, the Mashgiach asks how the beinoni can serve with them, and brings the advice that outward motions awaken inner feeling. This leads to the dispute between Chabad, who served with the mind, and the Polish tzaddikim, who sought hislahavus. Both are right, since each Jew follows his soul's root. The Mashgiach develops this through the counting of Bamidbar: every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah with an exact place, which explains why the son of the Israelite woman was refused a place in Dan's camp. He returns to chapter 16: understanding with the mind that one should love Hashem already counts.

en: The beinoni cannot control his heart, but he can and must know with his mind that he was created to serve Hashem.
Love and fear are the two wings that carry every mitzvah upward, and outward motions such as raising the voice can awaken the inner feeling.
Both Chabad's service with the mind and the Polish tzaddikim's hislahavus are true, because each Jew is drawn to the path of his soul's root.
Every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah, which is why Jews were counted by name and arranged by banner, tribe and family in their exact place.
Before Shavuos each Jew must see that his own letter in the Sefer Torah is kosher and beautiful.
If contemplation does not kindle love in the heart, understanding with the mind that one ought to love Hashem already counts in Heaven.

counting of the Jews in Bamidbar

title.en: The beinoni must know with his mind

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of Tanya chapter 16: the beinoni cannot rule his heart, so he must at least know with his mind that he was created to serve Hashem. A tzaddik feels love of Hashem, while the beinoni gets a taste only at times of favor, on Shabbos and Yom Tov, as King David asked to visit Hashem's palace.

title.en: Outward motions awaken the heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that love and fear are the two wings of every mitzvah and asks how a beinoni can serve with them. He brings the Mesilas Yesharim's advice that outward motions arouse inner feeling, illustrating with the raised voice of an excited person and with what psychologists say, and warns against strange motions.

title.en: Chabad and the Polish tzaddikim

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the dispute between the Chabad tzaddikim, who served with a cool mind, and the Polish tzaddikim, who sought hislahavus. He recalls an old Lubavitcher chassid who davened word by word with tears in the Stoliner shul in Williamsburg, mentions the Mitteler Rebbe's Kuntres HaHispa'alus, and asks who is right.

title.en: Each soul to its rebbe; Jews as letters

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that both are the words of the living G-d, each by its root. Hashem matches every talmid to the rebbe of his soul's root, as the heavenly voice decrees matches, and as souls stood together at Sinai. Every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah, and a single missing letter invalidates it.

title.en: Counted by names, not numbers

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Jews are counted in parshas Bamidbar before Shavuos: each Jew is a letter of the Torah, as the early sages were called soferim for counting its letters. They were counted 'by names', not numbers, like children who are called by name while cattle are branded with numbers, so that each Jew is set in his exact place.

title.en: The camps as the five books

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the arrangement of the banners: the camps correspond to the five books of the Torah, with the Kohanim and Leviim in the middle corresponding to Vayikra. The Leviim numbered twenty-two thousand, matching the twenty-two letters of the alef-beis, and every Jew stood by his banner as his soul is placed in the Torah.

title.en: The son of the Israelite woman

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the son of the Israelite woman was refused a place in Dan's camp when the desert was large, and answers that he was not a letter of the Sefer Torah. Even a ger can be a crown on the letters, as Rabbi Akiva, from a family of gerim, expounded the crowns, but according to the Gemara's other account this man mocked the lechem hapanim and was an apikores, so he had no connection at all.

title.en: Each Jew in his place before Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that before Shavuos each Jew must make his letter in the Sefer Torah kosher and beautiful, and returns to the dispute: every Jew belongs to his place, and Hashem arranges that each is drawn to Chabad, to Belz or to Rav Shach according to the family of letters his soul belongs to. Nothing is by chance.

title.en: Love of Hashem in the mind suffices

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Ba'al haTanya taught that the main thing is the mind, while others stressed the middos, and all are right. He reads Tanya chapter 16: one should contemplate Hashem's greatness in creation, which may kindle love and fear, and if it does not, understanding with the mind that it ought to be so is enough and is counted in Heaven as real love.

catalogTitle: תשובה על “כי קרוב אליך הדבר מאד” - איך אהבת ה' ויראת ה' קרוב לבינוני. די להם אהבה ויראה שכליות' בלי הרגשים גדולים שיש לצדיקים.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, on Tanya chapter 16, how serving Hashem stays 'very near' even for a beinoni who cannot feel love and fear in his heart: love and fear understood in the mind become the wings that lift his Torah and mitzvos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the title page of the Tanya, which is built on the verse 'ki karov eilecha hadavar meod', and recalls the earlier chapters: contemplating Hashem's greatness with chochmah and binah gives birth to love and fear, which comes easily to tzaddikim. For a beinoni whose heart does not catch fire, the Tanya in chapter 16 gives a great rule: love and fear that he understands with his mind are also enough. Along the way he speaks about true stories of tzaddikim, tells the Yismach Moshe's dream of tasting the Rambam's yiras shamayim, and describes the overwhelming fear of Reb Zusha, Reb Shlomo of Karlin and Reb Shmelke. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on why Hashem held the mountain over Klal Yisrael at Sinai, explains why Chazal say a good thought is 'joined' to the deed, and ends with the simple Jew whose hidden love lifts his mitzvos as far as olam haYetzirah.

en: The whole Tanya is built on the verse that serving Hashem is 'very near', and the Mashgiach shows how this holds for every person according to his level.
A beinoni who cannot bring his love and fear into the feeling of the heart still serves Hashem properly with love and fear understood in the mind.
When this understanding moves him to learn and do mitzvos, it becomes the wings that lift his Torah and mitzvos, as if he had served with felt love and fear.
By nature a thought of the mind cannot join a physical deed and lift it; Hashem joins them, and this is the meaning of 'a good thought Hashem joins to the deed'.
Mitzvos done from felt love and fear rise to olam haBeriah; those done from understanding are joined there by Hashem; those done from habit rise through hidden love only to olam haYetzirah.

candidateTopics: intellectual love and fear of Hashem

title.en: 'Very near' for each according to his level

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Tanya's title verse 'ki karov eilecha hadavar meod' and recalls how contemplation with chochmah and binah gives birth to love and fear, easily for tzaddikim. He asks what the beinoni should do, answers that understood love and fear are enough, and brings the Yismach Moshe that 'vachai bahem' means something different for each person's level. He then begins the text of chapter 16.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe tastes the Rambam's fear

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises true stories of tzaddikim as a way to bring a person close to Hashem, recommends the Tehilla LeMoshe, and tells the Yismach Moshe's dream in which he asked to feel the yiras shamayim of great figures and could not bear even the Rambam's fear from a time of katnus. He explains through the beat of the heart that every person goes through rising and falling.

title.en: The overwhelming feelings of tzaddikim

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the fear of Reb Zusha, the Ba'al HaTanya's words about Reb Shlomo of Karlin's constant fear, and Reb Shmelke, who had to be shaken out of his dveikus. He explains that tzaddikim felt this because their pure souls had no insulation blocking the current.

title.en: When the heart cannot feel

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya on one whose contemplation of Hashem's greatness never reaches the feeling of the heart. His mind still understands that his soul should yearn to Hashem, that the soul stays in the body like a living widow, and that Hashem is grasped only through Torah and mitzvos, like embracing a clothed king.

title.en: Understanding gives the mitzvos wings

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Tanya says understood love and fear are also good: the understanding moves a person to learn and do mitzvos, and it becomes the two wings that lift them, as the Zohar says. A thinking person could busy himself with other wisdom or chess; that his mind leads him to Torah gives his learning the same aliyah.

title.en: Why Hashem held the mountain over them

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's question why Hashem held the mountain over Klal Yisrael at Sinai after they said 'na'aseh v'nishma'. The Torah was given for all generations, including people who must force themselves to learn and serve; forcing oneself is good, and the coercion at Sinai was for them.

title.en: Hashem joins the good thought to the deed

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Chazal say 'a good thought Hashem joins to the deed' instead of the usual 'it is as if he did it', and answers that Chazal's words carry a second intention. Felt love comes from the physical heart and can lift the physical deed; a thought of the mind cannot by nature, so Hashem joins it, and the mitzvah rises to olam haBeriah.

title.en: The simple Jew's hidden love

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes a simple Jew who does mitzvos out of habit from his chinuch, without thought. His mitzvos still rise, because they come from the hidden love in every Jew, but only to olam haYetzirah. He closes with the idea that each mitzvah has many layers, and the inner part meant for olam haBeriah stays below.

catalogTitle: מדריגת יראה ואהבה בדרך 'לעשותו' - יכולים הכל לעשותו' חוץ רשעים עד שיעשו תשובה.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 17, the Mashgiach explains that the Torah's promise that serving Hashem is 'close, in your mouth and your heart, to do it' is kept through a love and fear born in the mind that lead to action, open to every Jew except a rasha until he does teshuvah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the difficulty Tanya chapter 17 resolves: the Torah says the matter is close 'in your heart', yet only tzaddikim rule their hearts. The answer, he explains, lies in the word 'la'asoso', to do it: a love and fear that the mind grasps through contemplating Hashem's greatness and that bring a person to act, even without feeling. He shows how the order of davening is built on this. The mind is in a person's control; only a rasha, whose heart rules him, cannot begin lasting avodah until he does the lower teshuvah, breaking the kelipah with a broken heart and raising the fallen lower hei. This leads to the exile of the Shechinah, the tale of Reb Zusha and the hay, and the Jew's inner exile. He then applies the chapter: when feeling is closed, as with the meraglim and Avraham's tenth trial at the akeidah, one must go with the mind. He ends with Tamuz and Av.

en: The Torah's 'close in your heart, to do it' refers to a love and fear that the mind grasps and that bring a person to keep the mitzvos, even when the heart feels nothing.
A person's mind is in his control even when his heart is not, so contemplating Hashem's greatness is within everyone's reach.
A rasha, whose heart rules him, cannot begin avodah that lasts until he first does the lower teshuvah, breaking the kelipah with a broken heart.
The lower teshuvah raises the fallen lower hei of Hashem's Name, which is the exile of the Shechinah.
When the heart is closed, even in the holiest place or moment, one must serve with the mind; this was Avraham's tenth trial and the trial the meraglim failed.

teshuvah tata'ah and the fallen hei

title.en: How can the heart be 'close'?

summary.en: The Mashgiach raises the difficulty with the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od, beficha uvilvavcha la'asoso': the Gemara calls fear of Heaven a small thing only for Moshe, yet the Torah is eternal, and only tzaddikim rule their hearts. He recalls that the previous chapter began the answer.

title.en: Love and fear in the mind; the order of davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews chapter 16: one who cannot arouse feeling in his heart still achieves enough when his mind understands, through contemplating Hashem's greatness, that one must love and fear Him. He shows how davening follows this path, from korbanos and ketores through the greatness of creation and the angels in birchos krias shema, up to ahavah rabbah and Shema.

title.en: 'La'asoso': the mind rules, except for resha'im

summary.en: Reading chapter 17, the Mashgiach explains that 'la'asoso' means a love that brings to action: the mind is in a person's control, so anyone can contemplate Hashem's greatness and reach an intellectual love that drives the mitzvos. Resha'im are different: they are in the power of their hearts, unlike tzaddikim whose hearts are in their power, so the Torah's words speak of living Jews.

title.en: A rasha needs teshuvah first; the fallen hei

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a rasha may do a mitzvah, even a great one, but it flares and goes out; to begin lasting avodah he must first break the kelipah through the lower teshuvah, the 'broken spirit' of the passuk as the Zohar reads it, which raises the fallen lower hei. He tells of Reb Zusha and the peasant's fallen hay, and distinguishes the lower teshuvah from the higher one.

title.en: The Shechinah in exile with the Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the exile of the Shechinah through Chazal's 'galu le'Edom, Shechinah imahem' and the passuk 'veshav Hashem Elokecha es shevuscha', which says Hashem Himself returns. On the level of remez, a Jew who acts like Edom drags the spark of G-dliness within him into exile in the kelipah; when he does teshuvah with a broken heart the kelipah breaks like a nutshell and the Shechinah rises from her fall.

title.en: When feeling is absent: Eretz Yisrael and the meraglim

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties the chapter back to the previous one: intellectual love and fear, without feeling, is also good, and one cannot always feel. He brings R' Avraham of Kalisk's warning to those traveling to Eretz Yisrael that they may feel nothing and must toil, and the Chasam Sofer's explanation of the meraglim's complaint that they had not felt the land's holiness, which they should have answered with tefillah.

title.en: Avraham's tenth trial and the meraglim

summary.en: The Mashgiach links the meraglim, the tenth trial of the generation of the desert, to Avraham's tenth trial. The akeidah's test was not self-sacrifice, which Avraham had shown long before, but a closed heart: he saw the Place 'from afar', full of questions and assailed by the Satan. The meraglim faced the same test in the land and did not know to break through the shell.

title.en: Serving with the mind when the heart is closed

summary.en: The Mashgiach draws the lesson of the two chapters: when the heart and feelings will not cooperate, one must go with the mind. Even at Ne'ilah or the height of Shabbos the heart may close, and that is Avraham's trial; every honest Jew who is not a rasha can serve this way, and one who finds himself in a rasha's state must break himself through teshuvah.

title.en: Tamuz and Av: the two eyes

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects parshas Shelach to blessing Rosh Chodesh Tamuz: Tamuz and Av, the 'days of the first grapes', are under the dominion of the sitra achra, given to Esav while Yaakov took the other months. They correspond to the two eyes, and are the months for breaking the sitra achra with a broken spirit.

catalogTitle: When Shabbos Ushers in ט' באב

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yirmiyahu was Shlomo HaMelech returned, so that Tisha B'Av is the day of Yirmiyahu and Shemini Atzeres the day of Shlomo, and when Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos, Shlomo comes back as the guest of Shalosh Seudos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Tisha B'Av that falls on Shabbos: the fast is pushed off and one may eat a meal like Shlomo's in his time, yet one stops eating at sunset while shoes may stay on. Since mitzvos work together like the organs of a body, he asks how Shabbos and Tisha B'Av can clash. He tells of Yirmiyahu buying Chanamel's field, and brings the Chasam Sofer: Chanamel hoped a tzaddik's land would be spared, while Yirmiyahu, a reincarnation of Shlomo who overslept on the day the Beis HaMikdash opened, felt he bore the guilt for the Churban. Hashem answered that a new body does not suffer for the old one. Shlomo wrote Shir HaShirim and Yirmiyahu Eichah; Shemini Atzeres is Shlomo's day of perfect union, marked by little eating, nezirus and Shabbos. At Shalosh Seudos of this Shabbos Shlomo returns, and the weeks to Shemini Atzeres turn Yirmiyahu back into Shlomo.

en: When Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos it is pushed off, and the Gemara allows a meal like Shlomo's in his time, yet one stops eating at sunset while shoes may stay on.
The mitzvos are like the organs of a body that work in harmony, so oneg Shabbos and the fast of Tisha B'Av cannot truly contradict each other.
Following the Chasam Sofer, Yirmiyahu was a reincarnation of Shlomo HaMelech and felt responsible for the destruction of the Beis HaMikdash he himself had built.
Tisha B'Av is the day of Yirmiyahu, the prophet of bitterness who wrote Eichah, and Shemini Atzeres is the day of Shlomo, who wrote Shir HaShirim, a day of perfect union.
When Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos, Shlomo HaMelech comes as a guest at Shalosh Seudos, and stopping to eat then is the closeness of that hour, not mourning.
From Tisha B'Av to Shemini Atzeres, Yirmiyahu's face is transformed back into Shlomo's, and the mourning is meant to become the black background of a woven picture of joy.

candidateTopics: Tisha B'Av that falls on Shabbos
Yirmiyahu as a reincarnation of Shlomo HaMelech
Shemini Atzeres as the day of Shlomo

title.en: Tisha B'Av pushed off by Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach says he wants to speak of the lighter side of Tisha B'Av, which this year falls on Shabbos and is pushed off; Rebbi even wished to abolish it then. He asks why one stops eating at sunset while shoes may stay on, and gives the simple answer that eating would spoil the whole fast.

title.en: Mitzvos in harmony like the organs of a body

summary.en: Citing 'mishpetei Hashem emes tzadku yachdav', the Mashgiach compares the 248 mitzvos to the organs of the body, which never contradict each other. He asks how there can then be a clash between oneg Shabbos and the fast of Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Yirmiyahu buys Chanamel's field

summary.en: The Mashgiach retells the prophecy that Yirmiyahu, imprisoned as Yerushalayim was falling, should buy his cousin Chanamel's field as a sign that fields will again be bought and sold, and bury the deeds in an earthen vessel. He then reads Yirmiyahu's prayer, protesting what purpose there is in buying a field that the Kasdim are about to take.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer on Chanamel's intention

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer: Chanamel knew the land would fall to Bavel, but believed punishment has no hold on a tzaddik, so he sold the field to Yirmiyahu while keeping its fruits for his lifetime. Yirmiyahu understood this and felt he was betraying him.

title.en: Yirmiyahu was once Shlomo

summary.en: From the seforim of Kabbalah the Mashgiach relates that Yirmiyahu was a reincarnation of Shlomo HaMelech, who overslept with the Temple keys under his pillow on the morning the Beis HaMikdash was to open. Yirmiyahu therefore felt he, more than anyone, was responsible for the Churban, and that Chanamel's 'insurance policy' was worthless.

title.en: A new body does not suffer for the old

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Yirmiyahu's prayer as a plea to the One who knows how sins pass from gilgul to gilgul: why must he betray his cousin? Hashem answers that He is the G-d of the body as of the soul; a new body that does not repeat the old sins need not suffer for them, a wonderful explanation of the Chasam Sofer.

title.en: Shlomo and Yirmiyahu, two faces of one person

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shlomo and Yirmiyahu are two faces of one person. Shlomo means perfection: his generation knew no war, hunger or poverty, a preview of the days of Moshiach and a perfect union; Yirmiyahu is its opposite, and remembering he was once Shlomo, he wrote Eichah instead of Shir HaShirim.

title.en: Shir HaShirim, Eichah and the Mishnah's 'come out and see'

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Shir HaShirim, a song of union, with Eichah, and explains that Eichah ends 'chadesh yameinu kekedem' as Yirmiyahu's longing to be Shlomo again; the Zera Kodesh distinguishes Yeshayah, prophet of consolation, from Yirmiyahu, prophet of bitterness. He reads the Mishnah at the end of Taanis as saying that on the fifteenth of Av one sees Yirmiyahu turned back into Shlomo.

title.en: Shemini Atzeres, the day of Shlomo

summary.en: The Mashgiach names Shemini Atzeres as the day of Shlomo: its haftarah is Shlomo's dedication of the Beis HaMikdash, the Bnei Yissaschar calls it the day of perfect union, and Shlomo is its guest after David. He asks why the verse describes Shlomo's era as 'each man under his vine and fig tree', and explains that the vine teaches the measure of nezirus and the fig the measure for carrying on Shabbos.

title.en: Nezirus, Shabbos and Shalosh Seudos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that nezirus is the joy of a tzaddik who needs little of this world, and Shabbos is union, the realm of the One as against the realm of the many; in Shlomo's time people lived this way rather than feasting. Shemini Atzeres, with its 'small meal', Koheles and the custom of hardly eating, expresses it, and so does Shalosh Seudos, the highest time of Shabbos.

title.en: Shlomo comes to Shalosh Seudos

summary.en: Returning to his question, the Mashgiach explains that when Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos, the guest at Shalosh Seudos is Shlomo HaMelech, as he was in his time, not as Yirmiyahu. Shabbos Chazon is the highest Shabbos of the year, and as its holiness grows toward sunset one stops eating as at Shemini Atzeres, out of union with Hashem, while shoes stay on because it is not mourning.

title.en: Consolation within the mourning

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Shabbos before Tisha B'Av reads Chazon Yeshayahu, from the prophet of consolation, because Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av. One fasts and weeps, yet the mourning itself is a consolation, as in the story of Napoleon; whoever mourns Yerushalayim merits and sees its joy, especially at Shalosh Seudos of this Shabbos.

title.en: From Tisha B'Av to Shemini Atzeres

summary.en: Bringing the Toras Avos, the Mashgiach explains that the Three Weeks through the Yamim Nora'im are one preparation for Shemini Atzeres: a 'plastic surgery' in which Yirmiyahu's face turns into Shlomo's. The verse 'atah hor'eisa lada'as' from the Tisha B'Av Torah reading is carried along and brought out again at Shemini Atzeres; Yeshayah and Shlomo are both of consolation and building.

title.en: Shlomo conquered the world with peace

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Shlomo as an emperor over the civilized world who, unlike Alexander or Napoleon, conquered with wisdom and peace, as Moshiach ben David will. When he judged the two women he had to send for a sword, since none was in the room; even his police went unarmed.

title.en: Male and female in holiness and impurity

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in holiness the masculine is the stronger and in impurity the feminine, referring to the Ohr HaChaim on Vayechi, and touches on why in the footsteps of Moshiach the feminine forces surface. Hence the land of Sheva was ruled by a queen; citing the Zera Kodesh, he says Sheva is spelled with a beis and denotes the attribute of fire and judgment.

title.en: Building through the mourning

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Queen of Sheva submitted to Shlomo in Yerushalayim, and reads the full spelling of Yerushalayim as Yirmiyahu becoming Shlomo again. Tisha B'Av, he concludes, is a day of sitting on the ground and weeping in order to build: within the full laws of mourning, every person should turn his inner Yirmiyahu into Shlomo, like a colorful bird woven on a black background.

title.en: Hashiveinu: preparing for the consolation

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every person lives through being Shlomo and falling to be Yirmiyahu, and the bitterness of Tisha B'Av is meant to serve his avodas Hashem. He closes with Eichah's last verse, the pain of a gentile rejoicing over the ruins, and a call to rise from the ground and prepare for the consolation and joy of the fifteenth of Av.

catalogTitle: נצחון היצר אינו אלא ע"י שמחה. ביאור “בכל עצב יהיה מותר.” עצות כנגד עצבות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, on Tanya chapter 26, that the yetzer hara is defeated only through zerizus that comes from simcha, and that sadness over sins belongs only at set times, 'by appointment only'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach learns Tanya chapter 26. A lazy, heavy fighter loses even to a weaker opponent, as a fierce lion overcomes a stronger ox; so too victory over the yetzer hara comes only through zerizus born of simcha, while atzvus, rooted in the element of earth, takes away the drive to fight. Quoting the Rebbe of Karlin, he says atzvus is no aveirah but leads to aveiros like nothing else. The passuk 'in all sadness there is profit' means only that sadness can lead to joy: regret over sins at set times, 'by appointment only', breaks the ruach hatumah and brings a joy greater than ordinary joy, like light from darkness. He roots simcha in bitachon, explains that suffering comes from the hidden, higher world and must be accepted with joy, and says that sadness during learning, davening or business is a trick of the yetzer hara.

en: Victory over the yetzer hara comes only through zerizus that flows from simcha; atzvus makes a person heavy and lazy.
Atzvus is not itself an aveirah, but nothing brings a person to aveiros as much as atzvus does.
Sadness over one's sins has value only at set times, and only because it leads to the joy that follows it.
Joy that comes after true sadness over sins is greater than other joy, like light that comes out of darkness.
Bitachon is the root of simcha: one who has someone to lean on rejoices, one who is forsaken is sad.
All suffering comes from the hidden world, higher than the revealed one, and is entirely for a person's good, so it is to be accepted with joy.
Sadness over sins that comes during learning, davening or business is a trick of the yetzer hara and must be pushed away.

title.en: Victory needs zerizus: the lion and the ox

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the coming chapters form one subject and begins Tanya chapter 26: in a physical fight, a lazy, heavy fighter is easily beaten even by a weaker opponent. He illustrates with a lion that overcomes a stronger ox or horse through its fierceness and energy, and reads that victory over the yetzer comes only through zerizus that comes from simcha.

title.en: Atzvus: heavy as earth, the way to aveiros

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that sadness and sluggishness stem from the element of earth, so a sad person lacks the drive to fight the yetzer hara, and brings the Beis Aharon quoting the Rebbe of Karlin that atzvus is no aveirah yet leads to aveiros more than anything. He then explains that 'in all sadness there is profit' does not praise sadness: nothing is created for nothing, and its only profit is the joy that can follow it.

title.en: Regret at set times, then true joy

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who regrets his sins with a bitter heart at set times breaks the ruach hatumah and comes to true joy, comparing it to a businessman who takes inventory of his assets and liabilities. He brings Tehillim 51, Dovid HaMelech's chapter after Nosson HaNavi came to him, which moves from a broken heart to a plea for joy, and the Arizal's custom to say it after Tikkun Chatzos.

title.en: Tikkun Chatzos and light out of darkness

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives the simple reason for the custom, to learn with joy after the sadness of Tikkun Chatzos, describes how Jews once rose at midnight to mourn the Beis HaMikdash, meaning inwardly the mikdash in each Jew's heart, and says today this is not for everyone. He explains that joy after sadness is greater, like light out of darkness, brings the passuk about not serving Hashem with joy, and says that one who did teshuvah may be sure Hashem forgave him, as the bracha 'chanun hamarbeh lisloach' shows.

title.en: Sadness by appointment only

summary.en: The Mashgiach dwells on the Tanya's words 'at set times': like a doctor who sees patients by appointment only, sadness over sins belongs only at fixed times, such as before sleep, erev Shabbos, going to the mikveh, erev Rosh Chodesh or erev Rosh Hashanah, and must otherwise be driven out. He adds that people today are small and this is hard for them, but it is good to know it and take hold of what one can.

title.en: Bitachon, the root of simcha: the two cows

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk 'for in Him our heart rejoices, for in His holy Name we trusted' and tells the story of R' Shimon of Yaroslav and his 'two cows', showing that bitachon is the source of simcha. Following R' Samson Raphael Hirsch's method of related sounds, he links simcha to leaning on someone and atzvus to being forsaken, which is why idols, which give nothing to lean on, are called atzabim.

title.en: Suffering from the hidden world; the port wine

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's advice against sadness over worldly matters, noting that people today are small but can use it at good times. He explains that one blesses for the bad as for the good and accepts it with joy, since it comes from the hidden world, higher than the revealed one, and tells how R' Shalom of Kaminka, after losing a child, asked for port wine, an expensive wine that tastes bitter to one who does not know it.

title.en: All suffering is for one's good

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the mashal: suffering comes from the hidden world and is entirely for a person's good, because Hashem loves His children and, as the Arizal writes at the start of Etz Chaim, created the world to do good. He brings the passuk 'those who love Him are like the sun going forth in its might' and the Gemara that three good gifts are acquired only through suffering, and concludes that even suffering must be accepted with joy.

title.en: Sadness during learning, davening and business

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that sadness over sins that comes during learning, davening or business must be pushed away, since it is not its time; it is the yetzer hara's trick, because sadness drives a person to taavos, as people unhappy at home console themselves with cake. Thoughts of sin belong at an appointed time, with reflection on Hashem's greatness, after which comes true joy.

catalogTitle: ע"י התבוננות יכולים להגיע ליראה ואהבה מוחית' וזה די למי שאינו יכול להגיע ליראה ואהבה מוחשית. ביאור על תשובה תתאה.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Tanya chapter 18: every Jew, even one who cannot reach love and fear through contemplation, carries a hidden love of Hashem inherited from the Avos, who were the merkavah (chariot) for the Shechinah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach recalls the previous chapter: contemplating Hashem's greatness, even when it brings only an understanding that one should love and fear Him, is already a level. Tanya chapter 18 adds that even a person of weak mind, who cannot reach this, can serve Hashem with a true heart through the hidden love every Jew inherits from Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov. He compares it to an inherited instinct in animals. The Avos were the merkavah, devoted to Hashem in every act, as were tzaddikim in every generation, illustrated by a story of the Chasam Sofer. He explains Yaakov's years with Lavan as freeing Jewish souls, the counterpart every tzaddik has in kelipah, and the hidden Leah and revealed Rachel. Since we are the Avos' children, even the lowest Jew holds the highest levels hidden, which may surface in his children, and each Jew can become a merkavah through his avodah.

en: Even a person who cannot contemplate Hashem's greatness enough to feel love and fear can keep the mitzvos and learn Torah from the depth of his heart, because of the hidden love in every Jew.
This hidden love is an inheritance from the Avos: love from Avraham, fear from Yitzchak, and the completion of both through Yaakov.
The Avos were the merkavah: they never turned their minds from cleaving to Hashem, and everything they did was devoted to Him; tzaddikim in every generation follow in this.

Since every Jew descends from the Avos, he too has an aspect of merkavah; even the lowest Jew receives at least the nefesh of nefesh of malchus of Asiyah, with chochmah and the light of Ein Sof hidden in it.
Through his avodah a Jew can bring this hidden aspect into the open and make himself, limb by limb, a merkavah for holiness.

candidateTopics: tzaddik and his counterpart in kelipah
Rachel and Leah as revealed and hidden

title.en: Even a weak mind can serve with a true heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of Tanya chapter 18 and recalls the previous chapter, that contemplation leading even to an understanding of love and fear is a level. He then explains that even a person who cannot contemplate at all can keep the mitzvos with a true heart, because of the hidden love inherited from the Avos.

title.en: The hidden love as an inherited nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew, as a descendant of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, has a hidden love for Hashem even if he does not feel it. He compares it to the instincts animals inherit, like an ox's desire for grass and a lion's for meat, which are part of their very being.

title.en: The Avos are the merkavah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Avos were the merkavah upon which the Shechinah rests, like the Beis HaMikdash in its time, bringing Yechezkel's vision and Yaakov's ladder in the week's parsha. He says tzaddikim in every generation, often hidden, live this way, and tells of the Chasam Sofer, who told his son that even moving a glass on the table was done only according to halachah.

title.en: Yaakov's work with Lavan's sheep

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Lechovitcher Rebbe, who would not say Torah on Vayetze because its plain story is itself the greatest Torah. He explains that Yaakov's years with Lavan and his work with the sheep were freeing Jewish souls from the sitra achra, and that Yaakov had to go to the land of the bnei kedem, the place of Bilaam, his counterpart.

title.en: Every tzaddik has a counterpart

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem made a balanced world, so every tzaddik has a counterpart in kelipah: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and the gentile sages, Avraham and Nimrod, who was killed the day Avraham died, Yaakov with Esav and Lavan. He then explains the Midrash's 600,000 sheep of Yaakov as the 600,000 Jewish souls, corresponding to the letters of the Torah.

title.en: Yaakov's flock, Leah and Rachel

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that the Yismach Moshe and the Apter Rav remembered being sheep in Yaakov's flock. He then explains Yaakov's fourteen years of work for Leah and Rachel as two aspects of the Shechinah, the hidden world and the revealed one, and places the hidden love of every Jew in the aspect of Leah.

title.en: Even the lowest Jew draws from the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya that the Avos are the merkavah and could draw souls to their children from all ten sefiros of the four worlds, and that even the lowest Jew receives at least the nefesh of nefesh of malchus of Asiyah. He explains the levels of nefesh, ruach, neshamah, chayah and yechidah, the ten sefiros and the four worlds.

title.en: Hidden greatness that surfaces in a child

summary.en: With the example of blond hair that skips a generation, the Mashgiach explains that the greatest levels lie hidden even in the lowest Jew, because the light of Ein Sof is clothed in the chochmah of every Jewish soul. He brings Sefer HaGilgulim that a simple Jew can father a great tzaddik, and explains that Hashem sometimes has a great soul born to an unlikely parent so the Satan will not interfere.

title.en: David's birth; every Jew can be a merkavah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that David HaMelech was born in a hidden way so the Satan would not stand in the way, since Moshiach comes from him. He concludes that every Jew, as a grandchild of the Avos, can bring out his hidden powers and make his limbs a merkavah, with the example of guarding the eyes.

catalogTitle: התחלת ביאור אהבה מסותרת. ישתדל להיות מרכבה לה' כפי יכולתו.

oneLiner.en: Opening Tanya chapter 17, the Mashgiach explains how 'the matter is very near to you' holds for every Jew: the mind rules the heart by nature, so service from understanding is always within reach, unless sin has taken away that control, and then teshuvah with a broken heart must come first.

abstract.en: Starting a new zman with chapter 17, the Mashgiach explains that the whole Tanya is built on the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od'. He reviews the earlier chapters: the Jewish soul naturally loves Hashem, as in the mutual love of Shir HaShirim, illustrated by the Avnei Nezer's reason about a bas Levi and by the Lechovitcher, who felt the moment his rebbe passed away. Hisbonenus in the morning brachos should bring forth love and fear, and where it does not burn Hashem counts the cold understanding as the deed. Chapter 17 asks how the Torah can call love of Hashem near when love of Hashem and love of this world cannot live together and only tzaddikim rule their hearts. The answer: the mind rules the heart by nature, so understanding-driven service of mitzvos is near to all, except a rasha who lost control, like Pharaoh. Such a person must first do teshuvah with a broken heart, raising the lower heh of Hashem's Name, which the Mashgiach illustrates with the lulav and esrog and with Yerushalayim and Rome.

en: The whole Tanya is built on the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od, b'ficha uvilvavcha la'asoso', to explain how serving Hashem is near to every Jew.
Because the soul is bound to Hashem, a Jew loves Him by nature and instinct, the mutual love Shlomo HaMelech describes in Shir HaShirim.
Love of Hashem and love of this world's desires cannot live in the heart together; one who is attached to this world only imagines that he loves Hashem.
The mind rules the heart by nature, so a love born of understanding that leads to doing the mitzvos is within reach of every person.
A rasha who sinned until his heart is no longer in his control cannot begin serving Hashem without first doing teshuvah with a broken heart.
Such teshuvah is the lower teshuvah, which raises the last heh of Hashem's Name from its fall and rejoins it to the other three letters.

title.en: A new zman: Tanya and 'ki karov'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why he starts the new zman at chapter 17, where the part on avodah begins, and asks newcomers to catch up on the earlier groundwork. He shows from the title page that the whole Tanya is built on the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od', explained at length and in brief for each person's level.

title.en: The natural love of a Jew for Hashem

summary.en: Reviewing the earlier chapters, the Mashgiach explains that the soul, a part of G-d above, loves Hashem by instinct, the mutual love of Shir HaShirim, which some say only on Pesach as the Minchas Elazar wrote. He brings the Avnei Nezer's reason why a bas Levi who remarried on false testimony is penalized: the tribe that stayed bound to Hashem at the Egel should have felt that her husband was alive.

title.en: The Lechovitcher feels his rebbe's passing

summary.en: Great tzaddikim felt their bond to Hashem, and even talmidim felt their bond to their rebbe. The Mashgiach tells how the Lechovitcher cried out that he was cut off from his rebbe at the moment Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin was killed, and calmed down once he was told, since a known reason is natural.

title.en: Hisbonenus in the brachos, and the cold intellect

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews how the mitzvah to love Hashem works: hisbonenus in the brachos of Krias Shema on the angels and on Hashem's love brings forth fear and love, the two wings of every mitzvah, before kabbalas ol malchus Shamayim. Where the flame does not catch, the earlier chapters taught that Hashem counts the cold understanding as if it were felt.

title.en: Chapter 17: is love of Hashem truly near?

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens chapter 17 and asks how the eternal Torah can say love of Hashem is near, when it does not always burn even in great people. Love of Hashem and love of this world cannot share one heart, and he brings the Kotzker's reading of the Targum on 'do not come near a woman' at Matan Torah: one cannot stand on both sides of the fence.

title.en: Only tzaddikim rule their hearts: the answer

summary.en: The Mashgiach strengthens the question from the Gemara that yirah is 'small' only for Moshe Rabbeinu and from Chazal that only tzaddikim have their hearts in their control. The Tanya answers that 'ki karov' means a love of the intellect that brings one to do the mitzvos: everyone with a mind can understand that he must keep the Torah, and this is accepted according to his level.

title.en: The mind rules the heart, unless sin removed it

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mind rules the heart by nature, over the left chamber where the animal soul nests, and can make a person do or refrain from anything if he stops to think. Only a rasha who never used that control loses it as a punishment; the 'reshaim birshus libam'. He brings Pharaoh, whose loss of bechirah at the plagues was the punishment for his earlier sins.

title.en: Teshuvah first: raising the lower heh

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'ki karov' speaks to ordinary people who have not lost their bechirah, while a rasha cannot begin a lasting avodah without teshuvah with a bitter, broken heart that breaks the kelipos. This is teshuvah tata'ah, raising the last heh of Hashem's Name from its exile; he connects it to the four species as the letters of the Name and tells the Rokeach's story of a dream about a separated heh, explained by a man holding the lulav and esrog apart.

title.en: Yerushalayim and Rome, and the separated heh

summary.en: When the soul's sparks are in exile within the kelipah, teshuvah breaks it and separates its forces. The Mashgiach brings Rashi that when one of Yerushalayim and Rome is full the other is ruined, and a remez from a Blazhever tzaddik on Yerushalayim written without a yud in Tanach; as long as the heh is apart the sitra achra is joined, and teshuvah reverses this.

catalogTitle: The Transformation of ט 'באב to שמיני עצרת and ירמיהו הנביא to שלמה המלך

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tisha B'Av is at its root a transformed Shemini Atzeres and Yirmiyahu a transformed Shlomo HaMelech, and that by transforming themselves Jews can turn Tisha B'Av back into the happiest day of the year.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach contrasts two opposite days: Shemini Atzeres, the wedding of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael and the day of Shlomo HaMelech, who attained everything he wished and lived a foretaste of the days of Moshiach; and Tisha B'Av, the day of Yirmiyahu, born on Tisha B'Av, who cursed the day of his birth and saw his mother Tziyon in disgrace. He reveals that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo, sent back to see the destruction of the Beis HaMikdash he built, so Tisha B'Av is at root a Shemini Atzeres. Through Zechariah's prophecy, the birth of Moshiach on Tisha B'Av, the haftarah of Sos Asis and the end of Eicha, he shows that the day will return to its glory. He applies this to the special calendar of the year and to the Shemini Atzeres maftir read before Yirmiyahu's haftarah, and closes: when the nefesh transforms through Torah, tefillah, middos and ahavas Yisrael, the zman transforms.

en: Shemini Atzeres is the climax of the year, the wedding of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, and its soul is Shlomo HaMelech, whose era was a sample of the days of Moshiach.
Every time has a soul that corresponds to it: Yirmiyahu, born on Tisha B'Av, is the soul of Tisha B'Av, as Shlomo is the soul of Shemini Atzeres.
Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, so Tisha B'Av is at its root a Shemini Atzeres that was spoiled and will return to its intended glory.
Eicha has a hidden meaning that will be revealed with Moshiach: beneath the lament lies the joy of the chassan and kallah, as in Shlomo's Shir HaShirim.
Because nefesh and zman correspond, when Jews transform themselves through Torah, tefillah, good middos and ahavas Yisrael, Tisha B'Av itself will transform.

title.en: Shemini Atzeres and Shlomo HaMelech's fulfillment

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with two opposite days, Shemini Atzeres and Tisha B'Av. He describes Shemini Atzeres as the wedding of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael and the day Shlomo HaMelech completed the Beis HaMikdash, attaining all he wished, which even Hashem's joy awaits until Moshiach; Shlomo's era and Shemini Atzeres are a sample of the days of Moshiach.

title.en: Tisha B'Av, Yirmiyahu and the mother in disgrace

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Tisha B'Av as a day of separation and churban whose soul is Yirmiyahu, born on Tisha B'Av, who cursed the day of his birth. He brings a Midrash: Yirmiyahu, who hoped to be a prophet of comfort, was like a kohen who uncovers the head of a sotah and finds his own mother; so Yirmiyahu saw Mother Tziyon in her disgrace.

title.en: Yirmiyahu as a gilgul of Shlomo

summary.en: The Mashgiach reveals that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech: because Shlomo married Pharaoh's daughter the night before the Beis HaMikdash was dedicated and rose late, it was decreed that he return to see its destruction. From this he concludes that Tisha B'Av is at root a Shemini Atzeres and will return to its intended glory.

title.en: Fasts that become festivals; Moshiach's day

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Zechariah's prophecy that the fasts of the fourth and fifth months will become days of joy, says Tisha B'Av is a lofty day now cloaked in mourning, and that Yirmiyahu will announce that he is Shlomo. He adds that Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av, reads tzom hachamishi as tzom hamashiach, and cites the Rambam that Moshiach descends from Shlomo.

title.en: Sos Asis and the hidden meaning of Eicha

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the last of the seven haftaros of consolation, Sos Asis, has Knesses Yisrael rejoicing in garments of salvation instead of black mourning clothes, and Yirmiyahu will bless the day he was born. He contrasts Shlomo's Shir HaShirim with Yirmiyahu's Eicha and says that with Moshiach the hidden meaning of Eicha, the joy of chassan and kallah, will be revealed.

title.en: Eicha written in tears; Yirmiyahu at the meal

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Yirmiyahu writing Eicha with ink mixed with tears, remembering the days when he was Shlomo singing Shir HaShirim. He shows that Eicha itself holds hope, that Hashem will not forsake forever and the plea to renew our days as of old, and portrays Yirmiyahu as the unseen guest at the seudah hamafsekes, weeping another year.

title.en: A special year: Tisha B'Av on Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach points to signs that this year is ready for the geulah: a Purim Meshulash in Yerushalayim, a haftarah of consolation on Shabbos Rosh Chodesh instead of one of lament, and an Erev Tisha B'Av on Shabbos when one eats a meal like the meal of Shlomo in his time. So one enters Tisha B'Av with hope.

title.en: Shabbos Chazon: seeing with the heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that on Shabbos Chazon one should see the Beis HaMikdash with the heart, as Shlomo said his heart saw, and that it is time to transform Tisha B'Av into Shemini Atzeres and Yirmiyahu into Shlomo. He brings the end of Mishnah Taanis, reading 'go out and see King Shlomo' as Yirmiyahu transformed, and the Ushpizin of Shlomo on Shemini Atzeres.

title.en: Shemini Atzeres maftir before Yirmiyahu

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that a small, low generation can bring the redemption with a little resolve. He notes that on the first Shabbos of the Three Weeks, usually Parshas Pinchas, the maftir is the Shemini Atzeres offering, read just before the haftarah of Divrei Yirmiyahu, to teach that Tisha B'Av must be transformed into Shemini Atzeres.

title.en: How to transform: nefesh and zman

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers how to transform: every Jew has a spark, and through Torah, tefillah, good middos and ahavas Yisrael the nefesh transforms and with it the zman. Tisha B'Av is called a moed because it has a future; he tells of a tzaddik who raised an empty cup on Tisha B'Av for the Kiddush to come, and closes with words to the bochurim joining a yeshiva and a brachah.

catalogTitle: כל הנשמות הם באים מחכמה שהוא למעלה מהשגה. אמונה מתלבש בחכמה. חידוש המסירת נפש של יהודי על מסירת נפש שיש פעמים אצל הגוים.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, on Tanya chapter 18, that every Jewish soul is rooted in chochmah, the point above understanding where the light of Ein Sof rests, and that this is why even the simplest Jew gives his life rather than deny Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the hidden love that every Jew has, since even the lowest soul is bound to chochmah ila'ah. Reading Tanya chapter 18, he explains that chochmah is not intelligence but the 'koach mah', the first point or flash from which understanding is built, like a drop that grows in the womb into a child. Because the light of Ein Sof rests in chochmah and no thought can grasp Hashem, emunah is above reason, and before Hashem everyone is a 'pesi' who believes. Emunah is a bond of feeling, like a mother's bond to her child, which is why even sinners have given their lives al kiddush Hashem throughout history, as in the story of the Shpoler Zeide's thieves. Non-Jews give their lives through indoctrination; Jews do so without it, from the root. He ends with Parshas Beshalach as the parsha of emunah, Hashem's faithfulness to Klal Yisrael, and Tu Bishvat as the yom tov of emunah.

en: Even the lowest Jewish soul is bound, level above level, to chochmah ila'ah, and therefore carries a hidden love for Hashem.
Chochmah is not intelligence but the source of intellect: the first point or flash, above understanding, from which binah builds a whole structure.
The light of Ein Sof rests in chochmah, and since no thought can grasp Hashem at all, emunah stands above reason and understanding.
Emunah is a bond of feeling and essence, like a parent's bond to a child, and such bonds are stronger than bonds built on understanding.
Therefore even the simplest and most sinful Jews have, throughout history, given their lives rather than deny Hashem.
Non-Jews give their lives through training and indoctrination, while Jews do so without being taught and without understanding, from the root of their soul.
Emunah also means faithfulness: Hashem is faithful to Klal Yisrael, and Parshas Beshalach, read near Tu Bishvat, is the parsha of emunah.
