title.en: Review: the hidden love in every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the previous chapters: every Jew, even the lowest, has a hidden love for Hashem, since his soul is bound level by level up to chochmah ila'ah. Having spoken of those whose love is revealed, the Tanya now turns to those in whom it is completely covered.

title.en: What chochmah really is

summary.en: Reading the Tanya, the Mashgiach explains that chochmah is not intelligence but the source of intellect, the first point above understanding, compared to the father's drop that the mother builds into a child. He illustrates it with the sudden flash of insight into a difficult Tosafos or Rambam, cites the Chovos HaLevavos that chochmah is close to prophecy, and the Arizal's reading of chochmah as 'koach mah'.

title.en: Emunah above understanding

summary.en: Since the light of Ein Sof rests in chochmah and no thought can grasp Hashem, emunah is above reason. The Mashgiach compares trying to grasp Hashem with the mind to trying to see music with stronger eyes, explains 'pesi ya'amin lechol davar' as a quality before Hashem, and brings Dovid HaMelech's words that he was like a beast before Hashem and thereby always with Him.

title.en: A bond of feeling and mesirus nefesh in history

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that emunah is a bond of feeling, like a mother's bond to her child, stronger than the bond of a teacher and student. Reading the Tanya that even the lowest Jews give their lives al kiddush Hashem, he recounts the generations of shmad: the expulsion from Spain, the refugees taken in by Poland, and whole communities killed in the Crusades with hardly any exception.

title.en: The Shpoler Zeide's thieves

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jew's mesirus nefesh comes from his emunah rooted in chochmah ila'ah, and tells of the thieves among the Shpoler Zeide's followers who were caught, tortured and killed al kiddush Hashem with joy rather than convert.

title.en: Non-Jewish self-sacrifice: training and indoctrination

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what is special about Jewish mesirus nefesh when non-Jews also give their lives, and answers that soldiers and others are trained and talked into it. He illustrates the old loyalty to a king with a story of a chassid of the Ba'al HaTanya who saw a soldier whipped for frozen ears, and of an old soldier who told the king that the service warms, not the blood.

title.en: Without understanding, from the root; emunah as faithfulness

summary.en: Continuing the Tanya, the Mashgiach explains that sinning Jews who were never taught and do not understand still refuse to deny Hashem, because Hashem's light rests in their chochmah, above reason. He adds that the word emunah means both belief and faithfulness, and that Hashem is faithful to the Jews as they are to Him.

title.en: Parshas Beshalach and Tu Bishvat: the time of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Parshas Beshalach is entirely about emunah, from the splitting of the sea to the war with Amalek, explains 'mah titzak elai' as Klal Yisrael's rescue coming from its root in atika, and mentions the custom of eating kasha. He closes with the Sanzer Rav's words on the yamim tovim from Tu Bishvat to Shavuos, and Tu Bishvat as the yom tov of emunah when the sap rises in the root.

catalogTitle: מסירת נפש של יהודי בא מחמת טבעו. (instinct) כי ה' שורשו.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, through Tanya chapter 19, that even the simplest Jew is ready to give his life for Hashem out of a nature above reason, like a flame that strains upward to its root.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the fact that even the emptiest Jews have given their lives for emunah, unlike gentiles who die for their causes only after being indoctrinated. A Jewish soul comes from chochmah, which is above daas, and there all Jews are equal; that is why Jews said 'na'aseh' without asking reasons. Tanya chapter 19 explains this with 'the candle of Hashem is the soul of man': every thing is drawn to its root, earth falls down and fire rises toward the element of fire. A flame strains upward although reaching its root would end it, because this is its teva, a word for what cannot be explained. So the soul longs to cling to Hashem. The Mashgiach applies this to Adar and Purim, when the lowest Jews show their bond to Hashem. He then explains that holiness comes from chochmah, which means bittul, while kelipah says 'I am something', and illustrates it with the kallah's bittul and with the merchant, the 'Canaani'.

en: Even the simplest and most sinful Jews have given their lives for emunah, which cannot be explained by indoctrination as it is among gentiles.
The Jewish soul is rooted in chochmah, which is above daas; there all Jews are equal, and their bond to Hashem works like an instinct.
Every thing is drawn to its root: earth falls to the ground, while fire strains upward to the element of fire beneath the sphere of the moon.
A flame strains upward although reaching its root would end its separate existence; this is its teva, a word for what has no further explanation.
Likewise the soul longs to part from the body and cling to Hashem, a longing that is above reason and comes from chochmah.
Holiness comes from chochmah and means bittul to Hashem, while kelipah is the feeling of being a separate 'something'.

candidateTopics: soul as the candle of Hashem

title.en: Why simple Jews give their lives

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that even the emptiest Jews have died al kiddush Hashem, contrasting this with gentiles who die for falsehood after being indoctrinated. He explains that the Jewish soul is rooted in chochmah, above daas, as shown by 'na'aseh' and by a mother's instinct for her child, and introduces Tanya chapter 19.

title.en: Every thing is drawn to its root

summary.en: Reading 'the candle of Hashem is the soul of man', the Mashgiach explains that all things are drawn to their root: solid things fall because they are mostly earth, like iron drawn to a magnet, while fire rises to the element of fire under the sphere of the moon. He shows from bedikas chametz at night how a flame pulls upward and flickers.

title.en: Fire, Torah and the soul that sways

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a gadol who identified a Jewish child exchanged with a gentile one by who would sway over the Gemara, because Torah is fire, and brings the Zohar that a Jew sways because his soul pulls upward. He reads the Tanya on the flame and asks why fire seeks to rise when it would be extinguished, against every creature's instinct of self-preservation.

title.en: The soul's longing is its nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the flame and the soul, with all its levels, long to reunite with their root although they would lose their existence there. He defines teva as the name for what cannot be explained further, illustrating it with a child asking his mother why things fall, and reads the Tanya that this longing comes from chochmah, above reason.

title.en: Adar, Purim and the lowest Jews

summary.en: Speaking of the coming Purim in Adar Sheni, the Mashgiach explains that Purim was made for the weakest Jews: the months descend from Nissan to Adar, Amalek attacks the stragglers, and in the Purim story the miracle came for the lowest Jews. Purim shows that even the smallest Jew is bound to Hashem above reason, which is why its mitzvah is drinking until 'ad delo yada'.

title.en: Chochmah as bittul, kelipah as 'I am something'

summary.en: Reading the Tanya that all holiness comes from chochmah, which is batel to Hashem, the Mashgiach explains that bittul and lowliness are the essence of a Jew, while kelipah says 'I am something' and is like chametz. He explains chochmah as 'ko'ach mah', the power of nothingness, and brings 'wisdom gives life' to show that chochmah is life.

title.en: Kallah, sitra achra and the merchant

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Klal Yisroel is batel to Hashem as a kallah to her chosson, while in the sitra achra the female is stronger, bringing the Or HaChaim on Vayechi. He then explains why a 'Canaani' means a merchant: the chesed of kelipah gives only in order to receive, unlike holy chesed which gives.

catalogTitle: אם אפי' קל שבקלים מוסר נפש לה'' למה היא חוטא? תירוץ - זה שטות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, on Tanya chapter 19, that even the lowest Jew is ready to give his life rather than deny Hashem because of the hidden love in his soul, and that he sins only because a spirit of folly enters him.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the Tanya's teaching that every Jew carries a hidden love for Hashem, so that even sinners give their lives for kiddush Hashem. This love comes from the chochmah of the G-dly soul, which in a sinner is like a glowing coal covered with ash. He then asks: if such a person is ready to die for Hashem, why does he sin all his life? The answer is folly, as people smoke knowing it shortens their lives. Only the spreading light of chochmah is in exile; its essence sleeps and wakes at a test of faith. He ties this to Adar and Purim, a month of hidden miracles for Jews whose faith is hidden. The Tanya adds that a Jew gives his life even over words or deeds he does not mean, a fear contained within love, like a mother holding her child on the stairs. The Mashgiach ends with a gloss of the Tzemach Tzedek limiting this rule.

en: Every Jew, even the lowest sinner, has a hidden love for Hashem that comes out when he is tested and ready to die rather than convert.
A Jew sins only because a spirit of folly enters him; sin is no more logical than smoking while knowing it kills.
Only the spreading of the soul's chochmah into the body is in exile; its root and essence stay untouched and only sleep.
Adar and Purim are the time of hidden miracles and of revealing the hidden love of even the lowest Jews.
A Jew gives his life even over a denial in speech or action he does not mean, because he fears being cut off from Hashem.
This fear is a fear contained within love, like a mother who grips her child on the stairs because she loves it.

title.en: The hidden love and the spirit of folly

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews that every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem, so that even the lowest are ready to die rather than convert. He reads the Tanya: this love comes from the chochmah of the G-dly soul, hidden in a sinner like a coal under ash, and covered by the kelipah through a spirit of folly.

title.en: Why he sins: it is folly

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why one who would die for Hashem sins all his life, and answers that it is folly. He compares it to smoking, which people do although they know it shortens life, something no animal would do, and traces this folly to Adam eating from the Tree of Knowledge.

title.en: Only the spreading light is in exile

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's distinction: only the spreading of chochmah into the body is in exile and darkened, while its root stays out of exile and only sleeps. At a test of faith it wakes, and even a simple Jew stands firm without reasons he can explain.

title.en: Nissan and Adar: open and hidden miracles

summary.en: Bringing the Sefer Yetzirah's parallel of world, time and soul, the Mashgiach contrasts Nissan, the month of open miracles, with Adar, the month of hidden ones. He shows that the Megillah's miracles are all within nature, yet perfectly timed by a higher hand.

title.en: Amalek, emunah and the melting of kelipah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Purim miracles were for sinful Jews whom Amalek could attack, and that Adar is for the lowest generation, whose faith is hidden. Moshe's strength against Amalek was emunah, and at a test of faith all the kelipos melt before Hashem like wax.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh over the garments of denial

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's point that the awakened love will not let the kelipah touch even the garments of thought, speech and action. Even a simple Jew forced to bow or to declare belief in idolatry gives his life, though he could say he does not mean it.

title.en: Fear contained within love

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how fear fits a teaching about hidden love, and answers with the Tanya's 'fear contained in love': a mother grips her child on the stairs out of fear that comes from her love. So a Jew fears harming his love for Hashem, by nature and by faith.

title.en: The Purim decree and the merit of the Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Haman's decree came because the Jews bowed to the image, and says the merit pleaded for them is their hidden love, which is above reason and is revealed in Adar. This is why one drinks on Purim and why simple Jews rejoice on Purim more than scholars.

title.en: Summary and the Tzemach Tzedek's exception

summary.en: The Mashgiach sums up that even the lowest Jew gives his life rather than deny Hashem, even in speech or action alone, because he feels it would tear him from his root. He then reports a gloss of the Tzemach Tzedek, which he heard of but did not see, that this has exceptions.

catalogTitle: Linking ט 'באב to פסח

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why Pesach fixes the day of Tisha B'Av through the rare trop pair kanei parah and yerach ben yomo: Av is the month of scattering and distance, and Nisan, a month that is fresh every day, serves it and will turn it into a month of joy.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the two trop notes, kanei parah and yerach ben yomo, that appear once in the Torah, in Parshas Masei on 'alpayim ba'amah', and asks why kanei parah sounds like a pazer and why they come as Av is blessed. By A"T B"Sh, the first day of Pesach fixes the weekday of Tisha B'Av; with the Maharal he explains that galus prepares geulah. The Bnei Yissaschar shows that Av, Shimon's month, draws its blessing from Nisan, Yehuda's month. Pazer means scattering, and a cow's horn is unfit for a shofar because it is made of segments: this is Av. The Shelah says every day of Nisan is like Rosh Chodesh, making Nisan a 'month fresh each day', like Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael. Midian sought to tarnish that love. Shlomo, who became Yirmiyahu, will again sing Shir HaShirim, and Av will become a month of joy.

en: By the A"T B"Sh sign, the weekday of the first day of Pesach fixes the weekday of Tisha B'Av, showing that Tisha B'Av is rooted in Pesach.
Galus is the preparation for geulah, and the geulah is rooted in the galus.
Av, the month of Shimon, has no blessing of its own and receives it from Nisan, the month of Yehuda, just as Shimon received his brachah and his nachalah through Yehuda.
Kanei parah, which sounds like a pazer, stands for Av, the month of scattering, while yerach ben yomo stands for Nisan, which serves it.
Nisan is a 'month fresh every day', like Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael, which never grows stale.
The avodah of the three weeks is to uncover the hidden love and the Moshiach concealed in Tammuz and Av, through Torah, tefillah, tzedakah and seeing the good in every Jew.

title.en: Two rare guests: kanei parah and yerach ben yomo

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces the trop notes kanei parah and yerach ben yomo, which appear only once in the Torah, in Parshas Masei on 'alpayim ba'amah'. He explains that yerach ben yomo serves kanei parah, and asks why kanei parah sounds like a pazer and why these notes come in the week Rosh Chodesh Av is blessed.

title.en: Pesach fixes the day of Tisha B'Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the A"T B"Sh sign of the Tur, by which the first day of Pesach fixes the weekday of Tisha B'Av. Pesach is geulah and Tisha B'Av is galus, and with the Maharal he explains that galus prepares the geulah; Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av, so Tisha B'Av is rooted in Pesach.

title.en: Yehuda and Shimon, Nisan and Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar: Nisan is Yehuda and Av is Shimon, and Shimon received his brachah and his nachalah through Yehuda, so Av draws its blessing from Nisan. He adds that the mazal of Nisan is a lamb and that of Av a lion, but the lion is rooted in chesed, and when Moshiach comes Nisan and Av will be revealed as one.

title.en: The Shabbosim of the three weeks and the meaning of pazer

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites the Rebbe of Lublin and the Divrei Chaim on the greatness of the Shabbosim of the three weeks and on the descent of the year from Shavuos to Tisha B'Av. Parshas Matos has seven pazers; pazer means scattering, which is galus, and the purpose of galus is to gather and bring back.

title.en: Why a cow's horn is unfit for a shofar

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah and Gemara in Rosh Hashanah that a cow's horn is unfit for a shofar because it is 'gildei gildei', made of segments, and looks like many shofros. The shofar stands for achdus and gathering, so a segmented horn, which is pizur, cannot serve; this is why kanei parah sounds like a pazer, and it is identified with Av, the month of galus.

title.en: Nisan, the month that is new every day

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Shelah that every day of Nisan has the kedushah of Rosh Chodesh. Using the kashrus rule of a ben yomo utensil, he explains that Nisan is a 'yerach ben yomo', a month fresh every day, called Aviv. Yerach ben yomo serves kanei parah as Nisan serves Av and Yehuda serves Shimon, and Nisan repairs the scattering of Av with achdus and geulah.

title.en: The shofar joins Av to Nisan; the third guest

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the shofar gathers the scattered and joins kanei parah with yerach ben yomo, and says that shofar spelled out in full equals in gematria kanei parah yerach ben yomo. Moshiach is born in Av, and the third guest this Shabbos is Chodesh Av itself, which comes to be blessed; he tells his listeners not to despair, for this month can be a partner with Nisan.

title.en: A love that never grows stale

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Nisan alone is entirely Rosh Chodesh, and answers that human affection begins as a flame and grows dull with time, but Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael stays as fresh as on the day of the chuppah. Nisan, the month of the chuppah, reveals that love, unlike a utensil in the laws of kashrus whose taste goes stale after a day.

title.en: Why the vessels of Midian needed kashering

summary.en: The Mashgiach raises the difficulty that the Torah requires kashering the vessels taken from Midian although a gentile's vessels are normally not ben yomo, and notes that the Chasam Sofer says there must be a hidden reason. He offers a reason of pshat: Balak, Bilaam and Midian sought to tarnish Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael, and Hashem's hatred for Midian is therefore always as strong as on the first day, so their vessels are always treated as fresh.

title.en: Hidden love in the three weeks

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the weeks of kanei parah there is a concealed love that surfaces on Shabbos, and that the fasts of the fourth and fifth months will become days of joy, as Zechariah says. Every Jew is Hashem's shaliach sent to distant places and times; he brings the Chasam Sofer that the seventeenth of Tammuz was the wedding of Boaz and Rus, and the Medrash that Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Betzalel, Shlomo and Yirmiyahu

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer, citing the mekubalim, that Shlomo HaMelech, whose wedding delayed the korban tamid, returned as Yirmiyahu to see the churban of the Bayis he built, and that Shlomo had earlier been Betzalel, who built the Mishkan. Betzalel's appointment required the people's consent as a king's would, and the same soul wrote Shir HaShirim and then Eicha.

title.en: Alpayim ba'amah: distance and nearness

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to 'alpayim ba'amah': alpayim carries yerach ben yomo, Nisan, and ba'amah carries kanei parah, Av. Alpayim ba'amah is the techum Shabbos, a measure of distance; in the three weeks the pazer becomes distance from Hashem, but underneath the kanei parah lies yerach ben yomo, and Av will be transformed into a month of geulah.

title.en: Kiddush on Tisha B'Av and the avodah of the three weeks

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Plancher Rebbe, who lifted an empty glass on Tisha B'Av and sang Kiddush, saying that when Moshiach comes we will make Kiddush on Tisha B'Av. The Moshiach hidden in Tammuz and Av must be uncovered through Torah, tefillah, tzedakah, ahavas Yisrael and seeing the good in every Jew, and he closes with Zechariah's promise that the fasts will become days of joy.

catalogTitle: אלו שעברו על חלב עכו"ם' חמץ בפסח' ונדה לא ימסרו נפשם על קידוש ה'. כל עבירה היא ע"ז ממש.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why sins tied to idolatry, like chametz on Pesach and niddah, weaken a Jew's readiness to give his life for Hashem, and begins Tanya chapter 20, which shows that every sin is rooted in idolatry and that Hashem remains exactly as He was before creation.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the previous chapter: even a simple Jew will give his life rather than bow to an idol, because idolatry tears him from his root. He then cites the hagahos of the Tzemach Tzedek, as he heard it: one who eats chametz on Pesach, drinks chalav akum, or is not careful with niddah may lose that readiness, since these sins are bound up with idolatry, and he uses this to explain a puzzling Tosafos about a tzaddik who drank wine a gentile had touched. He contrasts the soldier's trained self-sacrifice with the inner instinct of even the lowest Jews. Turning to Tanya chapter 20, he explains that Anochi and Lo yihyeh contain the whole Torah, that every sin is rooted in idolatry, and that everything is drawn to its source, a sense sins numb. He then explains Hashem's absolute oneness, unchanged by creation, through the parable of speech and thought within the soul.

en: A Jew will give his life rather than even outwardly bow to an idol, because he senses that idolatry tears him from Hashem, his root, and this is above reason.
Sins connected to idolatry, such as chametz on Pesach, chalav akum and niddah, can take away a Jew's readiness for mesiras nefesh.
Every sin is truly rooted in idolatry, so a Jew should be as ready to overcome his nature for any sin as for idolatry; he fails only because he does not understand this.
Anochi and Lo yihyeh lecha include the whole Torah: every positive mitzvah stems from emunah and every prohibition from idolatry, its opposite.
Everything is instinctively drawn to its source, so all creation and above all Jews are drawn to Hashem; sins dull this sense like an anesthetic.
Hashem is One exactly as before creation; creation brings no change in Him, since everything is as nothing before Him.

title.en: Self-sacrifice and the three exceptions

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that every Jew will give his life rather than bow to an idol, since idolatry is above reason and tears him from his root. He brings, as he heard it, the hagahos of the Tzemach Tzedek: one who eats chametz on Pesach, drinks chalav akum or is lax with niddah may not have this strength, because these sins are tied to idolatry.

title.en: A puzzling Tosafos; Jewish versus trained self-sacrifice

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story from Tosafos in Avodah Zarah about a tzaddik who drank wine a gentile had touched to annoy him, and who later gave his life al kiddush Hashem, and says the Tzemach Tzedek's words explain it. He then contrasts soldiers and others who are trained to die for a cause with Jews, even the lowest, whose hidden love would not let them be torn from Hashem.

title.en: Every sin is rooted in idolatry

summary.en: The Mashgiach outlines the coming chapters: being ready to die for idolatry while stumbling in other sins is foolishness, because every sin is rooted in idolatry. If a Jew understood this, he would overcome his nature for every sin as he does for idolatry.

title.en: Anochi and Lo yihyeh include the whole Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach begins Tanya chapter 20: the first two commandments, heard from Hashem Himself, include the whole Torah, the positive mitzvos stemming from emunah and the prohibitions from idolatry. To explain this, the Tanya first speaks of Hashem's oneness, and the Mashgiach explains 'all believe that He is alone' with the Rosh Hashanah piyut, where Hashem searches the hidden places of the heart.

title.en: Drawn to the source; the ox knows its owner

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that everything is drawn to its source, as hunger and thirst draw a person to what he lacks, so all creation is drawn to Hashem. Through the ox that knows its owner, the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and the Canaanite slave who may eat terumah, he shows how a person's soul extends into his possessions, and explains that sins numb a Jew's sense of Hashem like an anesthetic.

title.en: Alone as before creation: yachid umeyuchad

summary.en: Reading the Tanya, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem is alone after creation exactly as before, with no change. Physical things occupy a place and exclude another, and every thing can be divided, so nothing created is truly one; Hashem's 'echad' is a oneness without limit, and before Him all the worlds are as nothing.

title.en: The parable of speech, thought and the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's parable: one word is nothing compared to the power of speech, still less to thought, and less still to the essence of the soul. He shows that a person thinks in a language, but the first stirring, like hunger or a desire, comes from the soul itself before any letters, as with an animal that wants food without planning.

catalogTitle: הקב"ה ודיבורו אחד ממש. אלא לגבי נבראים יש צמצומים.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 21, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem's speech is not separate from Him as human speech is; it is one with His essence, and the tzimtzumim and concealments exist only from the side of the creations who receive.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach places chapter 21 within a five-chapter unit showing that any sin, even the smallest, cuts a Jew off from Hashem like idolatry, since Anochi and Lo yihyeh are the roots of all the mitzvos; the Ba'al Shem Tov, he notes, said this in one word. He then explains that human speech is communication that separates from the speaker and is felt, which the Ba'al haTanya could sense and which a tape recorder now shows, and he tells the story of the Ba'al haTanya and the king in prison. Hashem's speech, by contrast, is not separate from Him; it is called speech only as a mashal, as Dovid compared himself to a desert bird only in his loneliness. Like a person's desire in the heart before it becomes thought, Hashem's speech is one with His essence, and nothing changed through creation. Only from the side of the recipients are there tzimtzumim and hester panim; for Him darkness is like light, and like the kamtza whose shell is part of itself, His garments are Himself.

en: Chapters 20-24 of Tanya show that every sin, even the smallest, cuts a person off from Hashem like idolatry, because Anochi and Lo yihyeh are the roots of all the mitzvos.
Human speech is communication that leaves the speaker and becomes something separate from him; Hashem's speech is not separate from Him at all.
Hashem's word is called 'speech' only as a mashal: as human speech reveals hidden thought to a listener, His speech is the revelation of His light to the creations.
Like a person's desire in the heart before it becomes letters of thought, Hashem's speech is one with His essence, and creation changed nothing for Him.
The tzimtzumim and hester panim exist only from the side of the recipients, so that they can bear the light; for Hashem darkness is like light and His garments are Himself.

title.en: Every sin as idolatry: the Ba'al Shem Tov's word

summary.en: The Mashgiach places the chapter within a five-chapter unit explaining that any sin cuts one off from Hashem like idolatry, since Anochi and Lo yihyeh are the roots of all positive and negative mitzvos. He says these are deep chapters he will go through quickly, and notes that the Ba'al Shem Tov said all this in one word on 'and you will turn away and serve other gods'.

title.en: Human speech and Hashem's speech

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that human speech is the communication that carries one person's thought over to another, as 'yadber amim' means leading over, and it separates from the speaker. Hashem's speech is not separate from Him; it is called speech only as a mashal. He contrasts the Rishonim's answer that a Sanhedrin is fixed but its ruling goes out as separate, which cannot apply to Hashem.

title.en: Speech is felt: the Ba'al haTanya in prison

summary.en: Reading the opening of chapter 21, the Mashgiach explains that the Ba'al haTanya, with his fine senses, could feel the speech that leaves a person, which a tape recorder shows today. He tells how the king came in disguise to the Ba'al haTanya in prison and tested him on the time and on the number of coins from the table to the ceiling.

title.en: Why it is called speech: a mashal

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that nothing is separate from Hashem, since His glory fills the earth, and His speech is not like ours just as His thoughts are not ours. He asks why it is called speech at all and answers that it is a mashal for revelation, like Dovid's comparison to a desert bird, and that the ten utterances and all of Tanach are His speech. He then shows that human speech expresses thought, and thought itself comes from a deeper root.

title.en: Desire before thought: speech one with His essence

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every thought is stirred by a desire in the heart, as when a person wants to eat, before it becomes letters of thought. For a person, speech is a power of a power; for Hashem, speech is His very essence, united with Him as the desire is united with a person's self, and there is no change in Him through creation.

title.en: Two points of view: Creator and recipients

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Nefesh HaChaim discusses this at length: no place is empty of Hashem, yet a person relates to his things as real. There are two perspectives: from the Creator's side only His glory fills the earth, while from the recipients' side we live in a world of imagination. He asks how anything can exist after creation if before it there was only Hashem, and answers that for Him it is all the same.

title.en: Tzimtzumim only for the receivers; the kamtza

summary.en: Rereading the text, the Mashgiach explains that the many tzimtzumim and the hester panim exist so the creations can receive the light without being nullified, but before Hashem darkness is like light. With the mashal of the kamtza whose shell is part of itself, and the halachah that one's own hand is not a head covering while another's hand is, he shows that Hashem's garments are His own essence. He closes by saying he will stop here and review.

catalogTitle: הרמ"ח מצות הם רמ"ח איברין דמלכא. איברים בטלים לנפש לגמרי. כשעושים מצוה לשם שמים נעשה אז מרכבה לה'.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 23, the Mashgiach explains that the 248 mitzvos are called the 248 limbs of the King because they are fully nullified to Hashem's will, so that one who does a mitzvah becomes a chariot for it, and one who learns Torah becomes truly united with Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by recalling the Tanya's promise that serving Hashem is 'very near', and asks why it is so hard; the answer is the spirit of folly, which daas, holy understanding, removes. Turning to chapter 23, he cites the Tikkunei Zohar that the 248 mitzvos are the 248 limbs of the King, and stresses that this is a mashal, since Hashem has no body. He explains that the whole world is a mashal for spiritual matters, as Shlomo HaMelech's three thousand meshalim and Shir Hashirim show. Mitzvos are the inner will of Hashem, and all the upper worlds draw their life from the mitzvos done below. Just as a person's limbs obey his mind instantly, without deliberation, so the mitzvos and the body doing them are nullified to Hashem's will and become a merkavah, as the Avos were. Torah study is higher still: a full union with Hashem, even with the light that surrounds all worlds, hidden from us only by hester panim.

en: The Mashgiach explains that serving Hashem is truly easy, and what makes it hard is the spirit of folly, which daas hakedushah removes.
Calling the mitzvos the 248 limbs of the King is a mashal, since Hashem has no body; the whole physical world was created as a mashal for spiritual matters.
The mitzvos are the innermost will of Hashem, and all the upper worlds, even the angels, receive their life through the mitzvos people do below.
Just as a person's limbs carry out his mind's will instantly without deliberating, the mitzvos and the limbs that do them are wholly nullified to Hashem's will.
When a person does a mitzvah, his limbs become a merkavah, a chariot, for Hashem's will, a taste of the level of the Avos.
Torah study is more than being a chariot: since every halachah is Hashem's will and wisdom itself, the one who learns is truly united with Hashem.
We do not feel this union because of hester panim, the concealment caused by the body and by sins.

candidateTopics: 248 mitzvos as the limbs of the King
bittul of the limbs to the soul
Torah study as union with Hashem

title.en: If it is so near, why is it hard?

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the Tanya's promise to explain that serving Hashem is very near and easy, and asks why it is so hard; he answers with the spirit of folly and the need for daas. He then opens chapter 23 with the Tikkunei Zohar on the 248 limbs of the King, warning that Hashem has no body.

title.en: The whole world is a mashal

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that everything in the world is a mashal for a spiritual nimshal: Shir Hashirim, the Sfas Emes on reading it on Pesach, Shlomo HaMelech's three thousand meshalim, and even the sweetness of good foods as a mashal for the sweetness of Torah.

title.en: 248 limbs, 248 mitzvos and the tzelem Elokim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the 248 mitzvos are physical things, like tzitzis and tefillin, that hold spiritual lights beyond thought, and that man's 248 limbs correspond to them; this is the tzelem Elokim. The mitzvos are the inner will of Hashem.

title.en: The worlds live from our mitzvos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem's will to do good draws life into all the worlds through the mitzvos done below, so that the Jew who keeps mitzvos is the soul of creation. Washing the hands in the morning purifies his part of the world from the night, when Hashem's name does not rest on darkness.

title.en: Limbs wholly nullified to the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts a child or student who pauses before obeying with a person's limbs, which carry out the mind's will instantly. So too the mitzvos, and even the body doing them, are wholly nullified to Hashem's will with no separation.

title.en: Becoming a merkavah like the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the limbs doing a mitzvah become a merkavah for Hashem's will, as the Avos were at every moment. He illustrates the difference between contact and merkavah from the laws of tumah, and brings Yaakov Avinu, over whom Hashem stood as he slept.

title.en: Torah study: union, not only merkavah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that thought and speech in Torah are the soul's inner garments, and that every halachah, kosher or pasul, is Hashem's will itself; since Hashem and His wisdom are one, one who learns Torah is not only a chariot but truly united with Hashem.

title.en: Hester panim and the light of sovev

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why one does not feel this union, and answers with hester panim, using a father watching his sleeping child and a dentist's anesthetic. He adds that the union of a Jew learning Torah is greater than that of the upper worlds, reaching even the light that surrounds all worlds, and that not feeling it is what keeps him from being consumed.

catalogTitle: פרקי אבות: פרק ששי: The קדושה of צדיקים and the חשיבות of Learning תורה

oneLiner.en: Learning the sixth perek of Pirkei Avos, the Mashgiach explains the kedushah of tzaddikim, whose very names carry holiness, and the greatness of one who learns Torah lishmah, for whom the whole world exists and whom the Torah guards from sin.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens the added sixth perek of Avos and asks why the Mishnah names its Tannaim: a tzaddik who learns Torah lishmah becomes so holy that his name is Torah. A person's name is his neshamah, as Adam named each creature by its letters; sinners lose their names, as with Zimri and Cozbi, and Moshe called Dasan and Aviram by their righteous father's name. He then asks what the 'many things' are that one who learns lishmah merits. Holy things spoil easily, like wine, which stands for Olam Haba, and that reward is beyond what any navi saw. The whole world exists for such a tzaddik, and everything that happens in it is for the tzaddikim. Following Derech Hashem, he shows that mitzvos bring down blessing, Torah lishmah most of all. Such a person loves Hashem and people and is loved by both. Stories of tzaddikim who sensed forbidden food show how the Torah keeps him from sin.

en: A tzaddik who learns Torah lishmah raises himself until his name is Torah, so the Mishnah names him and mentioning his name is like saying words of Torah.
A tzaddik's name, and even the name of the place where he lived, carries his kedushah and can draw down a yeshuah for the one who mentions it.
The reward of one who learns Torah lishmah is so great that not even a navi saw it, and the whole world is worthwhile for him alone.
Everything that happens in the world, great or small, happens for the sake of the tzaddikim and Klal Yisrael, even when nobody knows why.
Mitzvos rise to Heaven and come down as blessing, aveiros come down as suffering, and the greatest blessing comes from Torah lishmah.
The one who learns lishmah has no interest of his own, so he loves Hashem and people alike and is loved by both.
The Torah he learns keeps him far from sin: Hashem gives such tzaddikim a special sense that warns them away from forbidden food.

candidateTopics: the world exists for the tzaddik
love of Hashem and love of Jews

title.en: Why the Mishnah names the Tanna

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces the sixth perek of Avos, added for the weeks from Pesach to Shavuos and written in the language of the Mishnah. He asks why the Tanna's name is mentioned at all, and answers that a tzaddik who learns lishmah becomes so holy that his name itself is Torah.

title.en: The power of a tzaddik's name

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the tradition that saying the word Berditchev helps a person in trouble, and the Gemara that mentions Chevron to recall the Avos, to show that even a tzaddik's place carries his holiness. He tells of a simple shoemaker who said the names of tzaddikim with every blow of his hammer.

title.en: A name is the neshamah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a person's name in loshon hakodesh is the root of his neshamah. Adam HaRishon did not invent names: he saw from each creature's nature which letters it was made of, unlike English names that mean nothing. A person who sins loses his name.

title.en: Losing a name: Zimri and Dasan

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the passuk at the end of Balak does not name the man and the Midianite woman during the sin but names them after Pinchas killed them: through the sin they lost their names and got them back afterwards. He brings a vort that Moshe called Dasan and Aviram 'sons of Eliav' to raise them through their father's name.

title.en: What are the 'many things'?

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads that one who learns Torah lishmah merits 'many things' and asks what they are, since the list that follows is said to be in addition. The Tanna does not say because he does not know: no eye has seen the reward of a talmid chacham. He begins to explain with the custom of covering wine from a gentile's look, since the holier a thing is, the easier it is spoiled.

title.en: Wine, Olam Haba and the power of a look

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that wine stands for the wine kept for Olam Haba, which is why Kiddush is made on it and why it is so easily spoiled. A tzaddik's look brings kedushah, as the Ramban explains about Moshe counting the Jews, and looking at the letters of the Sefer Torah at hagbah does too. Olam Haba is so holy that a gentile may not even look at it, and no navi saw the reward of one who learns lishmah.

title.en: The whole world is worthwhile for him

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the whole world was created for one who learns lishmah, bringing Ben Zoma's brachah over the crowds who serve him. To answer why Hashem keeps a world so full of reshaim, he gives the mashal of a merchant whose one returning ship pays for nineteen lost ones, and adds that roads are built so that a tzaddik can pass on them.

title.en: Everything happens for the tzaddikim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a tzaddik who smiled because he saw a king's castle, built by twenty thousand workers over twenty years, collapse after it sheltered a tzaddik from the rain for a few minutes. He applies this to the news: Vashti's death in Persia and Nixon's resignation happened for reasons known only in Heaven, and in the future the nations will claim reward for having built roads and houses for the Jews.

title.en: Mitzvos bring down blessing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why one who learns lishmah is called a friend, using the Derech Hashem: mitzvos rise to Heaven and return as blessing, aveiros as suffering, and Torah lishmah brings the greatest blessing. He brings Rashi that in the time of the Mabul even the animals were corrupted because of people, while Noach's portion of the world stayed good. He stops for time and promises to explain Torah lishmah further.

title.en: Loving Hashem and loved by people

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the love goes both ways: what a person is in Heaven he is below, as in the earlier Mishnah about one whom people are pleased with, and as the Maggid read 'know what is above is from you'. He brings the Midrash of a tzaddik whose coffin floated, with the passuk that one who offers all his wealth for such love is scorned, and explains it with the mashal of offering eighty-five cents for a Buick.

title.en: No self-interest, no machlokes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that people quarrel because each has his own interest, while in the days of Moshiach all will want one thing and form one band to do Hashem's will. One who learns lishmah never means himself, so he loves everyone. He resolves how one can love both Hashem and a fellow Jew without dividing the love: every Jew's neshamah is a part of Hashem, as is the Torah.

title.en: Kept from sin: the Beis Halevi and Yeshuos Yaakov

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who learns lishmah is never a ba'al ga'avah and has special help from Heaven to stay far from sin. He tells how the Beis Halevi did not eat a chicken later found to be treif, and how the Yeshuos Yaakov sensed that a pancake made in a fleishig pan was treif when it spurted in his face, since for a great tzaddik everything is a sign from Heaven.

title.en: The Vitebsker's fish in Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of Rav Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, the Maggid's leading talmid, whose going to Eretz Yisrael left the other talmidim to become Rebbes. In chutz la'aretz a fish swam into his gabbai's net for Shabbos; in Tzfas the heavenly calls to teshuvah kept him awake, and in Teveria the fish splashed the gabbai, which he explained by the strength of Eretz Yisrael's creatures.

title.en: Food that once had a shaylah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that the Chiddushei HaRim never ate anything on which there had been a shaylah, even when a Rav ruled it kosher, because even a havamina of treif leaves a trace of impurity, and he sensed it once when it was given to him. He adds a story of the Belzer Rav who refused fruit even though every halachic consideration permitted it.

title.en: The Slonimer Rebbe and the beard

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story he heard from a Slonimer chassid in his shtibel in Williamsburg who witnessed it: the Slonimer Rebbe ate supper at the home of a poor beardless Jew in Yerushalayim, refused the fish because the borrowed plates had not been toveled, and told the host and the bearded neighbor the difference between them. He concludes that Hashem helps tzaddikim know what is forbidden.

title.en: Mr. Singer and the Radziner gabbai

summary.en: The Mashgiach begins a story told to him as a boy by Mr. Singer, an honest man in his Williamsburg shtibel, whose father hosted the Radziner Rebbe's gabbai when he came to collect ma'amados. He starts the story over in brief.

catalogTitle: מעלת התורה על המצות שהיא יחוד ממש בין ה' ובינינו. אם עושה עבירה ח"ו הוי יותר גרוע מהסט"א ממש.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why learning Torah unites a Jew with Hashem even more than mitzvos, and why a sin, which cuts him off from Hashem's will, makes him worse than the sitra achra itself, which never rebels against its Creator.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews Tanya chapter 23: Torah study unites a Jew with Hashem more than other mitzvos, so Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai did not stop learning even for tefillah; the Arizal's statement that tefillah is central before Moshiach is like medicine for a sick man, not a ranking. Learning should bring great yirah, a yirah higher than the one that precedes learning, but most people today are numbed, like a patient under anesthesia, and do not feel it. Chapter 24 is the opposite: every sin, even against a rabbinic law, separates a person from Hashem's wisdom and is like idolatry, worse than the sitra achra, which obeys Hashem like Bilaam. The Mashgiach shows how Hashem has the sitra achra given a small share: the goat to Azazel, tefillin hair, thirty-nine lashes, no matzah on Erev Pesach and the Magen Avraham's custom about kiddush. He warns that such customs need good sense, and ends with the laws of the bathroom.

en: When a Jew learns Torah he is united with Hashem's wisdom in a way beyond even the highest angels, more than through other mitzvos.
The Arizal's teaching that tefillah is central in the time before Moshiach does not make tefillah greater than Torah; it is what the present condition needs.
Knowing that learning unites one with Hashem should bring a higher kind of yirah, but people of our generation are numbed and do not feel it, though the bond is real.
Every sin, whether a Torah or a rabbinic prohibition, separates a person from Hashem's will and wisdom and is truly like idolatry.
The sitra achra itself never rebels against Hashem, since it knows its life comes from Him, so a sinner is worse than the sitra achra.
Hashem wants the sitra achra to keep a small measure of life until Moshiach comes, so the Torah has something given to it without offering to it.

candidateTopics: Torah study as union with Hashem
tefillah in the time before Moshiach
kiddush and the hour of Maadim

title.en: Torah above mitzvos, and tefillah today

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews Tanya chapter 23: Torah study unites a Jew with Hashem beyond other mitzvos, which is why Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai did not interrupt even for tefillah. He explains the Arizal's teaching that tefillah is central before Moshiach with a parable of a sick man who needs orange juice more than bread and meat.

title.en: The great yirah that comes from learning

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's point that knowing how learning unites one with Hashem should bring great yirah, distinguishes the lower yirah before learning from the higher yirah within it, and uses this to settle the Gemara's two statements about Torah and yirah. He then explains why most people today do not feel this yirah, comparing them to a patient under anesthesia.

title.en: A sin, even a rabbinic one, cuts off from Hashem

summary.en: Opening Tanya chapter 24, the Mashgiach explains that rabbinic laws are also Hashem's wisdom, entrusted to the sages of each generation, and that according to the Arizal they come from an even higher root. Therefore any sin separates a person from Hashem's will and wisdom and is like serving idols.

title.en: Worse than the sitra achra itself

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in a sin the garments of the soul from kelipas nogah, and even the soul itself, become bound to the sitra achra. He then explains why the sinner is worse than the sitra achra: the Satan himself, with all his hosts, is subservient to Hashem and does His will.

title.en: Giving the sitra achra its small share

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Bilaam, who could not go against Hashem's word, and explains that the forces of evil depend on Hashem for their life. Hashem wants them to keep some life, and the Mashgiach shows this in Purim, the goat sent to Azazel as the Ramban explains it, the hair at the tefillin, kaparos, the thirty-nine lashes as the Chasam Sofer explains them, and the Bnei Yissaschar's reason for not eating matzah on Erev Pesach.

title.en: Kiddush in the hour of Maadim, with good sense

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Magen Avraham's custom not to make kiddush between six and seven on Friday night, the hour of Maadim, and the Aruch HaShulchan's sharp objection, and explains the Magen Avraham along the same line: the wine must not be taken wholly from the sitra achra. He adds that whoever keeps the custom must not make a hungry family wait, tells how the Chofetz Chaim made kiddush at once for a hungry guest, and concludes that everything must be done with sense.

title.en: The sitra achra's nourishment and the laws of the bathroom

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Mashgiach reads that the kelipos are subservient to Hashem and draw their life from the 'back side' of His will. He explains why the laws of the bathroom are part of the Shulchan Aruch: the sitra achra draws its life from the waste, and so one may not think words of Torah there. He closes that nothing in Hashem's creation is in vain.

catalogTitle: כמו שהטוב הכי גדול היא קיום המצוה' כן להיפוך' הדבר הכי גרוע היא עבירה. איכות עוה"ז יותר רע מטוב' חוץ אצל צדיק.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 24, the Mashgiach explains why a sin is worse than the kelipos and the lowest creatures, why this world is mostly evil and bitter except for the true servants of Hashem, and why a Jew who would die rather than serve idols still sins: a spirit of folly hides his hidden love.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the previous lesson: through a mitzvah a person is united with Hashem more than the highest worlds, while through a sin he is worse than the sitra achra, which still submits to Hashem; following the Ba'al Shem Tov, every sin carries a spark of idolatry. He then reads the Tanya's words that this world is the dregs of the kelipos, and shows from nature, from people and from each person's own reckoning that evil dominates here. Only rare tzaddikim truly taste the sweetness of Torah; he illustrates this with the Beis Aharon of Karlin, the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the cherries, and the tale of the king who sought a happy man's shirt. Returning to the text, he explains that the Tanya now answers how serving Hashem can be 'very near': a person sins only through a spirit of folly, which hides the love that would make him give his life rather than serve idols. Even wild animals obey Hashem, and they cannot harm one who keeps his tzelem Elokim.

en: Through a mitzvah a person is bound to Hashem more than the highest worlds, while a sin cuts him off and makes him worse than the sitra achra, which still submits to Hashem.
In the upper worlds there is no evil, in the lower worlds good is the majority, but in this world evil dominates over good.
Only rare tzaddikim truly feel the sweetness of Torah and mitzvos; most people's lives hold more pain than pleasure.
Wealth, power and status do not bring contentment; only one who serves Hashem with truth and trusts in Him is truly content.
Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem that would make him give his life rather than serve idols; he sins only because a spirit of folly keeps him from seeing that every sin is also idolatry.
Even the wildest animals carry out Hashem's will, so the sinner is worse than them; and an animal cannot harm one who keeps his tzelem Elokim.

candidateTopics: this world as dominated by evil
the sweetness of Torah and mitzvos

title.en: A mitzvah unites, a sin is worse than the sitra achra

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the previous lesson: through Torah and mitzvos a person is united with Hashem more than the highest worlds, while one who sins is the only creature that rebels against Hashem's will, worse than the sitra achra. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that thinking Hashem sees and lets the sin pass is a spark of kefirah.

title.en: This world, the dregs where evil prevails

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya that this world is the dregs of the kelipos, explains the difference between ordinary waste and pure dregs, and shows that evil, absent above and a minority in the lower worlds, dominates here. He illustrates it from animals, from people, and from each person's reckoning of his own life.

title.en: Tzaddikim taste the sweetness of Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the exceptions are tzaddikim who feel the pleasure of Torah that Dovid HaMelech describes, while most people are not zocheh to it. He tells how the Beis Aharon of Karlin compared a poritz's extravagant summer sleigh ride to his own delight in Nishmas, and brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the free cherry: a taste is given as a sample, then one must pay with toil.

title.en: The great and wealthy are not content

summary.en: The Mashgiach argues that this world is full of bitterness even for those who seem to have everything: world leaders, Napoleon who barely slept, the wealthy described in Likutei Moharan, and the statistics of suicide among the prominent. Only the Jew with bitachon who serves Hashem is content.

title.en: The king and the happy man's shirt

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story he heard as a boy: a melancholy king was told to sleep one night in a contented man's shirt, but the only truly happy man his messengers found was a laughing beggar who owned no shirt at all. Wealth and power, he concludes, bring no contentment.

title.en: Serving with truth, and the Tanya's opening question

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that one who serves Hashem with truth feels sweetness in a blatt Gemara, Tehillim, Shabbos and every mitzvah, but one should not expect the world itself to offer contentment. Returning to the text, he explains that the Tanya now begins answering its opening question from the title page: how can serving Hashem be 'very near'?

title.en: The sotah, the spirit of folly and the hidden love

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Chazal that no one sins unless a spirit of folly enters him, learned from the sotah. Every Jew, even a sinner, has a hidden love that would make him give his life rather than serve idols; he illustrates it with an angry father who snatches his child from a speeding car. So why does the sotah sin, when it is easier to resist adultery than to be killed?

title.en: A sin is worse than the lowest creatures

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the spirit of folly covers the soul up to chochmah but not chochmah itself, so idolatry awakens mesirus nefesh; in truth even a light sin is idolatry and makes the sinner worse than impure creatures. He brings the Gemara that a gnat preceded the wicked, and explains that wild animals, though they have no choice, do Hashem's will, and that no animal may rule over a man.

title.en: Tzelem Elokim: the wolves and Daniel

summary.en: An animal kills a man only when he appears to it like a beast, having lost his tzelem Elokim. The Mashgiach tells the Skulener Rebbe's family story of wolves that sniffed a wagon of holy children and left them unharmed, mentions Daniel in the lions' den, and concludes that the sinner rebels against Hashem more than the worst creatures, out of folly.

catalogTitle: זה ספר לבינונים. מהו בינוני. השקפה נכונה למחשבות ותשוקות בלתי נכונות. אהבה ויראה לנשמות קטנות. לימוד תורה בהתמדה.

oneLiner.en: Opening the Tanya as a 'book of beinonim', the Mashgiach explains that improper desires do not make a person less of an ehrlicher Yid, that the Tanya's short path to serving Hashem is meant for small people, and that even they can reach full, deep Torah learning through the hidden love every Jew inherits from the Avos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with the Tanya's three categories, tzaddikim, beinonim and reshaim, and explains that a person is created with a body and its desires in order to fight them: a desire for something improper means he is not a tzaddik, not that he is not an ehrlicher Yid, and the sin is only in letting the thought stay. He then reads the title page: a book for beinonim, gathered from seforim and from the Alter Rebbe's teachers, built on the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od', with a long way through chapter 17 for those who can contemplate with chochmah, binah and da'as, and a short way from chapter 18 for smaller people. Reading chapter 18, he explains that the Torah speaks to the smallest Jew too, so even he can keep all the mitzvos, including talmud Torah, the hardest of them. A digression on the Gemara about interrupting learning for the Megillah teaches that bittul Torah is a matter of quality as well as quantity. He closes with the hidden love inherited from Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, illustrated by a father who rescues his son from a fire.

en: A desire for something improper means a person is not a tzaddik, not that he is not an ehrlicher Yid; the sin is only in letting the thought stay in his head.
The Tanya, a book for beinonim built on 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od', explains this closeness in a long way through chapter 17 and a short way beginning in chapter 18.
The long way is the Chabad path of contemplation with chochmah, binah and da'as that gives birth to love and fear of Hashem; the short way is for those too small for it.
The Torah is eternal and speaks to the smallest Jew as much as to Moshe Rabbeinu, so even he can keep all the mitzvos, including talmud Torah.
Bittul Torah is a matter of quality as well as quantity: learning less deeply than one could is a kind of bittul Torah.
Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem inherited from the Avos, which comes into the open when his bond with Hashem is threatened.

candidateTopics: long way and short way in avodas Hashem
hidden love inherited from the Avos

title.en: Tzaddik, beinoni and improper desires

summary.en: The Mashgiach sets out the three categories of tzaddikim, beinonim and reshaim and explains that a person is created with a body and its desires in order to fight them. Having an improper desire means one is not a tzaddik, not that one is not an ehrlicher Yid; the passuk 'velo sasuru' addresses such people, and the sin is only in letting the thought stay.

title.en: The title page: a long way and a short way

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's title page: a book for beinonim, gathered from seforim and from the Alter Rebbe's teachers, built on the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od'. He explains the long way of chapters 1-17, the Chabad path of contemplation with chochmah, binah and da'as, and the short way from chapter 18 for people who cannot use it.

title.en: Chapter 18: the word 'me'od' and small souls

summary.en: Opening chapter 18, the Mashgiach asks how the Torah can call serving Hashem 'very near' when most people are not ovdei Hashem, and answers that the Tanya now addresses the person of limited understanding. He explains how chochmah and binah give birth to love and fear of Hashem, likened to a son and a daughter, and that this one cannot reach even the lower level of understanding it with his mind.

title.en: The Torah speaks to the smallest Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah is eternal and given to everyone from Moshe Rabbeinu to the smallest Jew before Moshiach, so even the smallest can keep all the mitzvos, even talmud Torah keneged kulam. Talmud Torah is the hardest mitzvah because every free moment, even a businessman's between customers, belongs to learning, and learning means understanding; reviewing a Gemara makes it clearer each time.

title.en: Bittul Torah in quality, not only quantity

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that one interrupts talmud Torah for the reading of the Megillah and asks why that is bittul Torah when the Megillah is Torah too. With the example of a shopkeeper who opens his store but serves customers lazily, he answers that learning less deeply than one could is itself a kind of bittul Torah, and returns to the Tanya's point that talmud Torah demands one's whole mind and heart.

title.en: The hidden love inherited from the Avos

summary.en: Back in chapter 18, the Mashgiach reads that even the small person can serve with his mouth and heart through the hidden love in the heart of all Israel, an inheritance from the Avos: love from Avraham, fear from Yitzchak, both from Yaakov. He illustrates it with a father angry at his son who still rushes into a fire to save him, and ends by announcing the schedule for next week.

catalogTitle: פרקי אבות: The Greatness of the חכמי התורה and the קדושה that Exists in their names

oneLiner.en: Learning the opening of the sixth perek of Pirkei Avos, the Mashgiach explains that the very names of the Chachamim are Torah, because a Jewish name is the substance of the neshamah, and mentioning it connects the learner to the Tanna himself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by comparing the exile of Klal Yisrael to Adam HaRishon's exile from Gan Eden, and says that young people, who are still in their own Gan Eden, have the opportunity to learn. He introduces the sixth perek of Avos, braisos about Torah written in the language of the Mishnah. Words of Torah said with ruach hakodesh contain far more than their plain meaning, so several explanations of one phrase are all true. He asks why the Gemara spends so much time repeating the names of the Chachamim, and answers that the name itself is Torah. Speech is powerful, as shown by the fruit of Eretz Yisrael in the days of the Midbar. He tells how Rav Shimon Sofer silenced scoffers in Krakow with a story about a holy name, brings the Mishnah's mention of Chevron on Yom Kippur, and explains with Adam's naming of the animals that a name holds a being's essence. Finally he explains why the Tanna does not spell out the reward of Torah lishmah: Olam Haba is too holy even for the Nevi'im to see.

en: Words of Torah said with ruach hakodesh contain much in few words, so several explanations of the same Chazal can all be true.
Mentioning the name of a Chacham is not an interruption in learning, because the name itself has become Torah.
Every word a Jew speaks has an effect in the world and above it: a good word builds and brings blessing, a bad word destroys.
A Jewish name is made of holy letters that are the substance of the neshamah, so mentioning a Tanna's name activates his neshamah and connects the learner to him.
The Tanna does not spell out the 'many things' that one who learns Torah lishmah merits, because his Olam Haba is too holy for even the Nevi'im to see.

candidateTopics: a name as the essence of the soul

title.en: Galus, youth, and the sixth perek

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Klal Yisrael's exile from Eretz Yisrael to Adam HaRishon's exile from Gan Eden, and says young people are still in their Gan Eden and can learn. He introduces the sixth perek of Avos, added before Shavuos, made of braisos about Torah written in the language of the Mishnah.

title.en: Why mention the names of the Chachamim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Torah said with ruach hakodesh contains much in few words, so several explanations are all true. He asks why so much time is spent repeating the names of the Chachamim, and answers that the name itself is Torah, reading 'baruch shebachar bahem' as praise of the one who devotes himself to them.

title.en: The power of speech

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every word a Jew says reaches the heavens: a good word brings light and bounty, a bad word destroys. He points to the huge fruit the meraglim brought back while Klal Yisrael learned Torah in the Midbar, and to Rashi's reading of 'yadber' as leading.

title.en: Rav Shimon Sofer and the holy name

summary.en: The Mashgiach says mentioning a tzaddik's name gives a hold on him, and that tzaddikim accomplished things through holy names. He tells how Rav Shimon Sofer, facing scoffers at his first drasha in Krakow, told of the Shabbos-desecrating factory owner in his father the Chasam Sofer's city whose factory burned when he pronounced a name his father taught him.

title.en: Chevron on Yom Kippur; a name is the neshamah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Moshe Rabbeinu killed the Mitzri with a holy name and that a tzaddik's name brings down chesed. He cites the Gemara asking why the announcement on Yom Kippur morning mentioned Chevron, and answers that naming the city of the Avos draws down rachamim; all the more the name of a Chacham, which is his very neshamah.

title.en: Adam's names and Rabbi Meir's neshamah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that the Chiddushei HaRim told a father to name his child himself so he would merit ruach hakodesh. He explains that Adam HaRishon named each creature by the letters it is made of, as with the aryeh, and that Rabbi Meir judged people by their names; so saying 'Rabbi Meir' before his halacha draws his neshamah into the learner and makes the halacha easier to understand.

title.en: Torah lishmah merits many things

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the braisa that one who learns Torah lishmah merits many things and is lifted above all creation. He asks why the Tanna does not say what the many things are, and answers that the Nevi'im described only the reward of those who help the talmid chacham; his own Olam Haba is too great for a living person to behold.

title.en: The holier, the easier to spoil

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains with the yayin hameshumar that the holier something is, the more easily it is spoiled: levels of tumah, meat versus vegetables, and wine that a goy touches. Olam Haba is so holy and so opposed to this world that no eye may see it, which is why the Tanna cannot describe it.

catalogTitle: שורש ומהות של אהבה מסותרת. הם ירושה מהאבות' האבות הם המרכבה' יראת ה' ואהבת ה' נתאחדו בגופם ונמשכו לבניהם.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Tanya chapter 18: every Jew carries a hidden love and fear of Hashem as an inheritance from the Avos, an instinct as natural as the inherited knowledge of animals, because the Avos were a chariot for the Shechinah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews how the first seventeen chapters of Tanya explain the verse 'ki karov eilecha hadavar meod' through contemplation, and opens chapter 18, which shows that even a simple person who cannot arouse love and fear can serve Hashem through the hidden love inherited from the Avos. To explain inheritance, he shows from nature that physical traits and instinctive knowledge pass to offspring (the bee's honeycomb, the beaver's dam, the spider's web) while acquired wealth and learning do not. A Jew's emunah is such an instinct, inherited from Avraham, whose creation completed the world. Sins can cover it, and people deny their belief to excuse their desires, as Esav and Chiel did. The Jewish body too is suited for kedushah; a convert receives a new body through tevilah, whose essence is self-nullification. Finally, love and fear are inherited because the Avos were a merkavah, wholly nullified to Hashem.

en: Tanya chapter 18 teaches that even a simple person who cannot arouse love and fear through contemplation can serve Hashem with them, through the hidden love inherited from the Avos.
In nature, physical traits and certain instinctive knowledge pass by inheritance, while things acquired from outside, like wealth or learning, do not.
A Jew's emunah is an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, part of his very makeup, so that even a Jew who says he does not believe really does.
Emunah can be weakened by sin, like a spoiled appetite, and people deny their belief to excuse their desires, but it can be restored.
The Avos were a merkavah, a chariot wholly nullified to Hashem, constantly in love and fear, and therefore drew their nefesh, ruach and neshamah to all their descendants.

title.en: Review and the opening of chapter 18

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews how the first seventeen chapters explain 'ki karov eilecha hadavar meod' through contemplating Hashem's greatness, which gives birth to love and fear. He then reads the opening of chapter 18: for a simple person, or a dulled generation, who cannot reach love and fear even intellectually, there is the hidden love in every Jew's heart, inherited from the Avos.

title.en: What passes by inheritance in nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in Hashem's nature traits pass by inheritance: hair color follows a known formula, a fine tree's seed gives fine fruit. Acquired things like money or knowing a masechta do not pass, but certain instinctive knowledge does: the bee's honeycomb, the beaver's dam and the spider's web are built by young that never saw their parents do it.

title.en: Emunah as an inheritance from Avraham

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a Jew's emunah passes by inheritance from Avraham Avinu, so every Jew believes instinctively, while a non-Jew must come to belief through contemplation and resists because it does not suit him, as the nations refused the Torah. Apart from rare exceptions of a misplaced soul, even a Jew who says he does not believe carries the belief in his blood.

title.en: Weakened emunah and self-deception

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares emunah to appetite: a spoiled stomach dulls it, and sins can weaken emunah, but a tzaddik, a mussar sefer or teshuvah restores it. He then shows how people deceive themselves and blame anything but themselves, with the hammer, yeshiva bochurim, Esav taking Machalas, a man of desire who claims heresy, and Chiel of Beis HaEli who rebuilt Yericho and explained away his children's deaths.

title.en: The creation of Avraham and the letter hei

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that after 'Vayechulu' creation was not yet complete: Chazal read 'behibaram' as 'b'Avraham', a new creature who believed in Hashem instinctively. The hei, which the Zohar calls the letter of birth, was added to his name so his emunah would pass to his children, as the morning verses say 'v'samta shmo Avraham' and 'his heart was faithful'. That emunah can be covered, like a spoiled stomach, but it remains.

title.en: The Jewish body and the hidden love

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jew's body comes from kelipas nogah and is suited for kedushah, its 248 limbs matching the 248 positive mitzvos. The love is revealed or hidden, but a great test awakens it even in a rasha. He then reads the Tanya text: from Avraham the trait of love, from Yitzchak fear, from Yaakov mercy, and the hidden love in the heart of all Israel is our inheritance.

title.en: The convert's new body and the mikvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a convert has a Jewish soul but a body born of a non-Jew, and through milah and tevilah receives a new body. Bringing the Baal Shem Tov's kavanos of mikvah from the Baal HaTanya's siddur and the Arizal, he explains that tevilah is a rebirth through self-nullification, like a curled-up fetus. He rejects a shortcut of many quick tevilos with a finger, and says one should do teshuvah before Shabbos as if converting anew.

title.en: The Avos are the merkavah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's question: how can love born from contemplation be inherited, and how can fear, its opposite, be included in it? The answer is that the Avos were the merkavah: never separated from Hashem for a moment, always in love and fear, wholly nullified like a chariot to its rider, and more than the mashal shows. Therefore they drew their nefesh, ruach and neshamah, with emunah that includes love and fear, to all their descendants forever.

catalogTitle: יש יראה ואהבה ביחד רק בה'. אבות נתאחדו בה' יותר ממרכבה גשמית. לפי שהאבות היו בעצם אלקות לכן בניהם גם הם כן. אין מקיף אם אינו מחובר לפנימיות. ביאור קצרה בד' עולמות וי' ספירות.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 18, the Mashgiach explains why love and fear of Hashem can live together only with Hashem, how the avos became so united with Him that this bond passed to their children, and gives a short explanation of the four worlds and the ten sefiros.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews that every Jew inherits a hidden love from the avos: love is the trait of Avraham and of Beis Hillel, fear that of Yitzchak and of Beis Shammai. Positive mitzvos come from love and prohibitions from fear, which is why a positive mitzvah overrides a prohibition, as he shows from the Ramban on zachor and shamor and from the Gemara on tzitzis and shaatnez. He then asks how fear, the opposite of love, can be part of the same inheritance, and answers that only with Hashem can union and awe coexist. The avos were Hashem's merkavah, yet more united than a chariot with its rider; their bond became their very essence and so passed to their children, together with nefesh, ruach and neshamah, even where these remain hidden as a makif. Finally he explains the ten sefiros and four worlds through the mashal of vapor, steam, water and ice, and the human powers of the soul, ending with daas.

en: Love is the trait of Avraham and Beis Hillel, fear the trait of Yitzchak and Beis Shammai; positive mitzvos stem from love and prohibitions from fear.
A positive mitzvah overrides a prohibition because love is greater than fear.
Love and fear can coexist without contradiction only toward Hashem: union with Him and nullification before Him go together.
The avos were completely nullified to Hashem, more united with Him than a chariot with its rider, and so they drew down nefesh, ruach and neshamah to their children.
Only a trait that is part of a person's essence is inherited; the avos' bond with Hashem became their essence, so their children inherit a hidden love.

The ten sefiros come down through the four worlds of Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah by ever greater tzimtzum, like vapor that becomes steam, water and ice, and in man they become the ten powers of the soul.
Daas is the bridge between the intellect and the midos: it knows when to use each trait.
